Global caveats

Issue Reading note
Segments were redefined in Q1 2026 Vehicle and eMobility became one Mobility segment. The FY2025 10-K presents five segments; the 2026 10-Qs present four with history recast. Every pre-2026 Mobility figure here is Vehicle plus eMobility summed.
Segment margin is not an EBIT margin Corporate absorbs all intangible amortisation, all net interest, all restructuring charges, all acquisition and divestiture costs and the non-service pension component. The 24.5% FY2025 segment margin compares with 19.0% of computed GAAP operating margin, and FY2026 guidance is GAAP EPS $10.36–$10.56 against adjusted $13.40–$13.60.
The data-centre metrics appear only outside the filings Data-centre revenue growth, content per megawatt, the 307 GW US pipeline, the megaproject tracker and the negotiation pipeline are disclosed on earnings calls and in analyst decks. None appears in a 10-K or 10-Q, none is defined by Eaton, and none reconciles to a reported line.
Mobility is inside continuing operations until Q1 2027 Roughly 10% of revenue and 6% of segment profit leaves in the Dana Reverse Morris Trust. FY2026 reported figures still include it, and Bloomberg's CY2027 consensus revenue still includes about three quarters of it.

Two further facts bear on the whole document. Boyd Thermal closed on 12 March 2026, inside Q1, and contributed $524m of sales and $121m of segment operating profit from that date to 30 June 2026. And the SEC XBRL extract for Eaton reports annual revenue as zero for FY2010–FY2016 and diluted EPS as zero for every year; every figure below comes from the filings.

1. Business description, model and unit economics

Eaton sells engineered hardware that moves, protects, conditions and cools electricity, plus aerospace fluid and electrical systems and vehicle powertrain components. It reports four segments after the Q1 2026 recast. Electrical Americas and Electrical Global sell one product catalogue split by where the equipment is made and sold; Aerospace sells content designed onto an airframe; Mobility sells drivetrain content designed onto a vehicle platform and is being separated into Dana.

Electrical Global 6,084 6,248 6,815 25% +3% +9%
Aerospace 3,413 3,744 4,249 15% +10% +13%
Mobility (Vehicle + eMobility) 3,601 3,452 3,109 11% −4% −10%
Total 23,196 24,878 27,448 100% +7% +10%

Source: 10-K FY2025, Note 18; 10-K FY2023 for the FY2023 column.

Electrical accounted for 79% of FY2025 segment operating profit at a 26.4% margin, Aerospace 15% at 23.9%, and Mobility 6% at 13.0%.

1.1 What each franchise sells and how the revenue arrives

Electrical. The revenue is disaggregated one way, into catalogue Products shipped from stock through distribution and configured Systems quoted against a specification and built to order. Systems is where the growth is.

$m 2020 2022 2023 2024 2025 5-yr CAGR
Electrical Americas — Products 2,255 2,732 2,949 3,009 3,205 7%
Electrical Americas — Systems 4,425 5,765 7,149 8,426 10,070 18%
Systems share of Americas 66% 68% 71% 74% 76%
Electrical Global — Products 2,608 3,424 3,462 3,493 3,885 8%
Electrical Global — Systems 2,095 2,424 2,622 2,755 2,930 7%

Source: 10-K FY2022 and FY2025, Note 3.

Systems is not the same as revenue recognised over time. The FY2025 10-K states that sales recognised over time were approximately 7% of consolidated net sales in 2025 and under 5% in 2024 and 2023, against Systems at $13,000m or 47% of consolidated sales.▪ Almost all of Systems transfers control when the assembly ships. A Systems order therefore sets its price at booking and incurs its cost at shipment, months later. That interval is the mechanism behind the 2026 margin decline in §13.

Route to market is two-step distribution plus direct sales to OEMs, utilities and large end users. Six large electrical customers accounted for 22% of the two segments' FY2025 sales, about $4,420m, an average of roughly $740m each; Eaton identifies them only as a group.▪ The wording of that disclosure changed in the FY2021 10-K from "large distributors" to "large customers", and the CEO described the same shift on the Q2 2026 call: "In the past, we were just primarily a distribution model. Now we have strong distribution and strong direct accounts." Per named account the exposure rose from 2.3% of Electrical sales in 2016 to 3.7% in 2025.

Backlog counts firm-committed orders only. The 10-K states that a significant portion of open orders are not firm because they have historically been subject to customer release, so the disclosed order book is the committed subset.▪ Total company backlog was approximately $24.1bn at 30 June 2026, of which 71% is targeted for delivery within twelve months. Customer prepayment is small: deferred revenue was $1,159m, about 5% of backlog.

Aerospace. Content is qualified onto an airframe or engine programme under the type certificate, then sold across a twenty- to thirty-year production run and a longer maintenance tail.▪ Eaton discloses one axis, market channel.

Source: 10-K FY2020, FY2022, FY2025, Note 3; 10-Q 2026-Q2.

Aftermarket passed OEM for the first time in H1 2026 at $920m against $864m and supplied 57% of the half's revenue growth.▪ Industrial and other is industrial filtration and golf grips, which moved into Aerospace in the Q1 2020 reorganisation when Hydraulics was sold; it is a quarter of the segment and responds to industrial machinery utilisation, with no aviation driver. Military contracts are primarily fixed-price with no performance-based or progress payments, so Eaton funds the working capital of its defence programmes.

Mobility. Contracting is release-based against blanket purchase orders, so there is no backlog, no book-to-bill and no order series. FY2025 revenue split $1,448m Vehicle Commercial, $1,056m Vehicle Passenger and Light Duty, $604m eMobility. Roughly 23–25% of revenue is aftermarket sold through the Roadranger network into the installed truck parc, sized at about $715m by Eaton's Q4 2025 deck and about $800m by Dana on the 11 June 2026 M&A call. Customer concentration is the highest in the company: four vehicle OEMs took 37% of FY2025 Vehicle sales and one OEM took 18% of eMobility sales.▪

1.2 What sets price, volume and cost

Eaton has declined to split price from volume since at least 2023. What it discloses is the organic bridge, the end-market mix and the order metrics.

Price in Electrical is set by published multiplier schedules on Products and at the project bid on Systems, and it is recovered through general list increases with a lag. Eaton took general increases effective 15 January and 1 April 2026 plus discrete increases, and pulled the Electrical Global general increase forward from Q4 to Q3 2026. Management's own framing of pricing is inflation recovery: "our industry historically has gotten price, and I would say that we're probably back in a more historical pattern of getting price each year" (Q3 2024 call). In Aerospace price is set at down-select and fixed by long-term agreement; the CEO told the March 2025 investor day that "prices historically for decades have been very sticky, especially in aerospace and electrical businesses. So think about the growth ahead of us more of a volume play than a price play as things normalize." In the same answer he added that Eaton does not expect to give price back.

Volume in Electrical is set by how fast Eaton can build and ship. Electrical Americas backlog reached 1.05x trailing-twelve-month segment revenue at 30 June 2026 against 0.78x at the end of 2023, with book-to-bill at 1.3 and trailing organic orders up 41%. Eaton is spending more than $1bn across two dozen Electrical Americas capacity projects, of which twelve are complete and ramping, six come online by the end of 2026 and six run beyond 2027. Revenue per work day rose about 25% from the start of 2025, including 8% from Q1 to Q2 2026.

The cost curve is dominated by metal. Eaton names iron, steel, copper, nickel, aluminium, lead, silver, gold, titanium, rubber, plastic, electronic components, chemicals and fluids as its major raw materials and gives no spend figure. Two independent inversions of the disclosed margin bridges against published copper prices put direct commodity and raw-material input at 18–21% of Electrical Americas revenue, roughly $2.4–2.8bn on FY2025 revenue [estimate: FY2025 bridge — 380bp of commodity and wage inflation on $13,276m less an estimated wage component at 35,000 employees; H1 2026 bridge — 470bp on $7,551m annualised; each divided by the blended basket move implied by COMEX copper up about 18% in 2025 and about 37% year over year in H1 2026]. Eaton hedges almost none of it: its own market-risk disclosure states that a hypothetical 10% move in commodity prices would produce a gain or loss of less than $1 million, against Vertiv's disclosed $15.8m on roughly 37% of Eaton's revenue.▪

Realised operating leverage in Electrical ran 44–50% incremental in FY2023–FY2024, 29% in FY2025 and 12% in H1 2026 excluding Boyd.▪ Aerospace converted $1,210m of added revenue into $308m of added profit over 2022–2025, a 25.5% incremental margin against a 23.2% starting margin, so three years of 40% revenue growth moved that segment's margin 70 basis points.

Two drivers are claimed and not yet visible in revenue. The 800-volt DC architecture and the medium-voltage solid-state transformer have produced no revenue: as of the Q1 2026 call Eaton had "more than a handful" of solid-state transformer pilots and was quoting 800-volt projects, with orders guided to H2 2026 and shipments to late 2027 and early 2028. And the claim that content per megawatt rises with AI architectures has no realised figure behind it. Eaton's stated addressable content per megawatt went from $1.2–1.5m to $3.4m, but $0.5m of the step arrived with Boyd's cooling portfolio in March 2026, and Eaton has never disclosed realised revenue per megawatt.

Segment gross margin is not disclosed. Allocating selling, administrative and research expense to each segment and solving for cost of products sold gives implied gross margins of roughly 44% for Electrical Americas, 32% for Electrical Global, 38% for Aerospace and 22% for Mobility, summing to $17,050m of implied consolidated cost of products sold against $17,131m reported, a 0.5% variance [estimate: SG&A and R&D intensities set so the four segments reconcile to reported consolidated cost of products sold; sensitivity is roughly one point of segment gross margin per point of SG&A intensity]. Electrical Americas has the highest gross margin in the company and converts about 30 cents of every revenue dollar into segment profit; Electrical Global converts about 19 cents.▪

Two figures cannot be derived. Products and Systems margins do not solve: setting uniform margins across both geographies gives a 37.6% Systems margin and a 5.7% Products margin, and a catalogue containing Tripp Lite, residential load centres and wiring devices does not earn 5.7%. The 1,050 basis-point gap between Electrical Americas and Electrical Global is regional scale and cost position, so the Products/Systems split cannot serve as a margin proxy. And Aerospace cost of products sold and research expense are not disclosed at segment level and are not derivable, so no per-ship-set cost column can be built.

Working capital scales faster than revenue. Days sales outstanding went from 60 at the end of 2024 to 69 on annualised H1 2026 revenue; inventory rose from $4,227m to $5,417m; unbilled receivables tripled from $330m to $1,015m. Deferred revenue nearly doubled to $1,159m and customer deposits collected rose 50% in FY2025, which offsets part of it. A voluntary third-party supply-chain finance programme inside accounts payable held $669m of obligations at 30 June 2026, with $1,126m of invoices confirmed in H1 2026 alone, so payables and cash-conversion ratios are not comparable to peers without adjustment.

2. Key technologies and technical differentiators

Eaton's 10-K names the methods of competition in Electrical as "performance of products and systems, technology, customer service and support, and price" — technology is one of four terms, listed alongside service and price, and the sentence is verbatim identical in the FY2016 and FY2025 filings. Reported research and development expense was $797m in FY2025, 2.9% of sales, up 0.4% in a year when sales grew 10.3%, and 2.7% of sales in H1 2026, the lowest in the ten-year series. Over the same period Eaton committed $11,164m to Boyd Thermal, Ultra PCS and Resilient Power, roughly twelve to fourteen years of research expense at the FY2025 run rate. The technology position Eaton presents to investors in 2026 was substantially purchased, and the Boyd purchase-price allocation says so: $7,190m to other intangibles and $3,733m to goodwill against $196m of property, plant and equipment.▪

Medium-voltage solid-state transformers and the 800-volt DC architecture. Power arrives at a data centre as medium-voltage alternating current, steps down through a copper-wound transformer to low-voltage AC, distributes through switchgear and busway, and is rectified at the rack. A solid-state transformer replaces the wound transformer with a power-electronics stage that converts the utility feed straight to DC, so the DC flows to the rack with no further conversions.▪ Eaton's CEO puts today's best AC designs at 93% efficiency and 800-volt DC at 98%; SemiAnalysis puts the same architecture at 82.0% baseline reaching 87.4%, a 5.4-point gain (newsletter.semianalysis.com, accessed 2026-08-17) [web]. The improvement is about 5 points in both accounts; the absolute levels differ by about 11 points and no source reconciles them.

Eaton started organic solid-state transformer work about three years before February 2026 and then bought the position. The CEO's account at the UBS conference on 2 December 2025: "we said, can we look outside? Is there anyone ahead of us? And the answer was like, we don't know. Let's go check and they found out that [Resilient] was actually a couple of years ahead of us. So we're accelerating that development." Eaton acquired Resilient Power Systems on 6 August 2025 for $86m — $55m of cash at closing plus $31m contingent on 2025–2028 revenue and technology milestones, with up to $50m of employee incentives on the same milestones. Eight months later the CEO described Eaton as "clearly ahead in terms of technology after the acquisition of Resilient Power last year." Both statements are Eaton's, eight months apart.

The competitive position is real and it is not exclusive. Eaton's JP Buzzell co-chairs the Open Compute Project's Power Distribution Sub-Project with ABB's Paolo Catapane, and the two companies committed jointly to a white paper on large-scale low-voltage DC architecture and component specifications [web]. NVIDIA's 800-volt DC ecosystem post names nine data-centre power-systems partners — ABB, Eaton, GE Vernova, Heron Power, Hitachi Energy, Mitsubishi Electric, Schneider Electric, Siemens and Vertiv▪ (developer.nvidia.com, accessed 2026-08-17) [web]. Co-chairing an open standard gives Eaton influence over the architecture and specifies it in public so components are interchangeable. On timing, IEEE Spectrum reports Vertiv's 800-volt DC ecosystem commercially available in the second half of 2026; Eaton guided to first orders in H2 2026 with shipments from late 2027 [web]. Eaton's Electrical CTO puts mass adoption in 2028–2029, so the architecture Eaton claims leadership in becomes dominant largely after the 2030 targets are due.▪

DC circuit protection. Alternating current crosses zero volts 100 or 120 times a second and a mechanical breaker interrupts at that crossing. Direct current has no zero crossing, so the arc must be extinguished actively and far faster. The CEO names DC breaker technology as one of four capability blocks required to win 800-volt DC work. ABB's SACE Infinitus is described in ABB's own materials as the world's first fully IEC 60947-2 certified solid-state circuit breaker up to 2,500 A, with a breaking time under 25 microseconds [web]. Eaton's medium-voltage hybrid breaker is a research programme funded through ARPA-E with IIT and Virginia Tech; Eaton sells DC moulded-case breakers today for photovoltaic, UPS and battery duty. Eaton's differentiated asset in this block is simulation — the CTO calls Eaton's plasma models "absolutely outstanding" for designing both AC and DC breakers — and the Breaktor resettable DC switching device developed for electric vehicles and reused into industrial and data-centre applications.

Silicon-carbide power conversion. Silicon carbide switches at higher frequency and temperature than silicon, which shrinks the magnetics and heat sinks. Eaton's 2025 investor-day deck states the 9395XR UPS gets "40% higher power density" from silicon carbide and is "99% efficient with Energy Saver System"; Eaton's own product literature gives 99% in Energy Saver mode, up to 97.5% in double conversion, and a footprint up to 30% smaller than similar models. Vertiv's PowerUPS 9000 and Schneider's Galaxy VXL both publish up to 97.5% double-conversion and up to 99% eco-mode efficiency. On published specification the efficiency gap against the two closest listed competitors is zero, and each of the three claims the smallest footprint against a different baseline.▪ The distinctive feature is EnergyAware, which releases part of the UPS battery back to the utility for frequency regulation so the asset earns revenue between outages; Eaton discloses no attach rate, installed megawatt count or revenue for it.

Liquid cooling. A GPU dissipating on the order of a kilowatt inside a 100 kW–1 MW rack cannot be air-cooled. A cold plate bolts to the chip and moves liquid through microchannels shaped to that chip's thermal map. Two barriers are named consistently: the plate is co-developed against a chip twelve to twenty-four months before launch, so a supplier absent when the chip is specified waits for the next generation, and the simulation capacity to work with the silicon providers is scarce. Eaton's CEO states Boyd is "the market leaders for liquid cooling, if you think about the cold plates and the CDUs." TrendForce names four cold-plate suppliers — Cooler Master, AVC, Boyd and Auras — and reports that sidecar coolant distribution units, the larger half of that market, are led by Delta, with in-row units supplied primarily by Vertiv and Boyd▪ (trendforce.com, accessed 2026-08-17) [web]. Boyd delivered $524m of sales at a 23.1% margin from 12 March to 30 June 2026, with Q2 revenue of $432m running 20% above Eaton's own guidance, and full-year 2026 revenue raised to $1.8bn against $1.1bn in 2025.

The reversal that prices the capability is dated. At the March 2025 investor conference the Electrical COO said cooling "is not a far adjacency for us" and the CTO said "organically, we have a tremendous amount of capability in cooling even today... there are unique patents that we hold in the cooling space, especially on thermosyphon and thermal management on heat sinks." Eaton signed for Boyd on 2 November 2025 and closed at $9,549m on 12 March 2026.

Modular and prefabricated power. Fibrebond and the 49%-owned NordicEPOD build the whole power block into a factory-made enclosure. The constraint relieved is field labour: "there is scarcity of people to work on a stick build. So there is a push towards more modular solutions. This is exactly why we last year decided to make the acquisition of Fibrebond" (Q2 2026 call). The technical barrier is manufacturing and project management, and the CEO says so. Modularisation also standardises the deliverable, which makes a second source easier for the customer to qualify.

Digital design and Brightlayer. The substantiated internal capability is engineering productivity: the 2025 deck claims a 50% reduction in design time and engineering cost versus the previous generation, worked through the UPS development cycle, and a 50% increase in sales-engineer productivity from an AI specification reader. These are cost and cycle-time claims, unverified outside the company, and they show up in margin and time-to-market. Brightlayer is the software platform. At the March 2021 investor conference Eaton committed to "$500 million of incremental revenue run rate through digital and software solutions" by 2025 from a zero base, reaffirmed it in March 2022, and the March 2025 conference held in the target year does not mention the figure. Brightlayer's last appearance on an earnings call was Q1 2024.

Aerospace additive manufacturing. On Bell's FLRAA programme, additively manufactured hydraulic swivel, scavenge pump and hydraulic filter module components delivered 30% weight reduction, 156 components consolidated or eliminated and 80% material waste reduction, and Eaton content on FLRAA is more than 8x its content on the Black Hawk. Weight is what an airframer pays for. FLRAA is entering production, so none of it is in realised revenue.

Utility grid-edge hardware. The three-in-a-box vacuum fault interrupter combines transformer, medium-voltage switchgear and controller in one SF6-free unit, which Eaton describes as self-disruption of its own transformer line. Eaton is also explicit about where it does not differentiate: "We are a bit more selective on single-phase transformers because it's the smallest part of our portfolio, also the least differentiated" (Q1 2026 call).

What the technology is worth in price. Electrical Americas segment margin declined from 29.5% to 27.5% year over year in Q2 2026, with a 470 basis point commodity drag against a 260 basis point volume benefit and no disclosed price or productivity offset, while organic revenue grew 18%. The recovery is running through calendar list-price actions and case-by-case increases. That is catalogue-industrial pricing behaviour with a lag. On the other side, the acquired technology runs at or above segment margin: Boyd at 23.1% inside Electrical Global's 19.8%, Ultra PCS at 27.9% inside Aerospace's 22.8%.

The roadmap base rate. Two prior technology-platform commitments have run their course. eMobility was launched in 2018 as the vehicle to scale power electronics into mobile markets, targeted at $1.2bn of 2025 revenue at 11% margin in March 2022 with the bar marked "Booked ~87%", raised to $1.5bn in October 2023, and delivered $604m with a $14m operating loss.▪ Brightlayer's $500m digital revenue target has no published outcome. Across the same period Eaton beat every consolidated financial commitment it set, by wide margins. The pattern is consistent: consolidated financial targets are met and discrete technology-platform revenue commitments are missed. Both the 800-volt DC and solid-state transformer positions are today unshipped.

3. Competitive advantages and moat assessment

3.1 Electrical

Eaton's Electrical business earns a real excess return on the capital it operates and holds a position that took decades and four large acquisitions to assemble. Return on capital employed excluding goodwill and acquired intangibles has been between 28% and 39% in every year since 2016 except the 2020 divestiture-and-COVID year, and was 38.9% in FY2025 on a company-wide basis.▪ Segment operating margin rose from 15.9% in 2017 to 26.4% in 2025 and segment profit grew from $2,003m to $5,295m. Data-centre revenue has grown above 35% for eight consecutive quarters and grew 65% organically in Q2 2026 against a market management sizes at 23%, which is share moving from someone.

The advantage is defensible now and open to erosion, and 2026 is the first period that tests it against equally-resourced rivals under cost stress instead of under scarcity. The excess return is amplified by a sold-out market as much as by a durable edge.

Pricing power failed its own test in the most recent quarter. Eaton's consolidated gross margin declined 350 basis points year over year in Q2 2026, from 37.0% to 33.5%, and Electrical Americas margin declined from 29.5% to 27.5% while organic revenue grew 18%.▪ The MD&A bridge for that quarter shows a 470 basis point decline from commodity inflation offset only by 260 basis points of volume, with no price and no productivity contribution disclosed. Medium-voltage switchgear is reported effectively sold out through 2028 in many channels and power-transformer lead times run about 128 weeks (getuniqcli.com, accessed 2026-08-17) [web]; a supplier with pricing power in that environment prices ahead of copper.

The same-quarter comparison against the two rivals of comparable scale went against Eaton. ABB's Electrification business grew revenue 19% to $5.2bn in Q2 2026 and expanded operational EBITA margin 100 basis points to 24.9%. Schneider Electric's Energy Management segment grew 18% organically and expanded adjusted EBITA margin about 100 basis points organically to 22.4% in H1, absorbing a 120 basis point net hit from raw materials, pricing and tariffs with 240 basis points of productivity. Vertiv expanded adjusted operating margin 410 basis points to 22.6% on 18% organic growth. Eaton's combined Electrical margin declined 172 basis points to 24.5% on 18% organic growth. The Eaton premium over ABB Electrification moved from +330 basis points in FY2024 and +290 in FY2025 to −40 basis points in Q2 2026.▪

And capital allocation is converting an excellent operating return into an ordinary corporate one. Boyd Thermal cost $9,549m net of cash. On its stub economics and Eaton's own $1.8bn full-year revenue figure, Boyd generates roughly $415m of segment operating profit, about 3.3% after tax on the price paid, against a cost of capital estimated at 8–10%▪ [estimate: risk-free near 4.2%, equity risk premium 4.5–5%, beta 1.1–1.2, after-tax cost of debt about 3.5%, debt roughly 10% of capitalisation]. Goodwill and other intangibles rose from $20,823m at 31 December 2025 to $32,840m at 30 June 2026, 58% of total assets and about 1.6x book equity. Company return on capital employed was 13.8% in FY2025; applying FY2025's operating margin to 2026 consensus revenue against the post-Boyd capital base gives about 10–11%. Return on the tangible operating base held at 33.7% annualised on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, so the decline in company return comes from the price paid.

Management claims: the 2025 investor day set out five sources of advantage — a partner network of consultants, EPCs, installers and distributors that "is not easy to recreate"; whole-life service on the installed base; portfolio breadth from substation to chip; global reach; and five core technology domains reused across eight end markets. On the Q2 2026 call the CEO defined the entry requirement for 800-volt DC as four capability blocks plus a service network that can "show up in a site in an hour, not in days", and concluded "it's not for everyone. It is not for every company."

Eaton's own filing: the Electrical competition paragraph names price as a principal method of competition and claims only that Eaton is "considered among the market leaders" — wording unchanged from FY2016 to FY2025. On intellectual property the FY2025 10-K states that management believes the loss or expiration of any single intellectual property right would not by itself have a material effect on any business segment.

What management concedes: lead times are extended on named product lines and Eaton is "going to knock them down time by time" (Q2 2026); pricing is inflation recovery reverting to a historical annual pattern (Q3 2024); working capital is behind peers on payables and inventory (CFO, 2025 investor day); manufacturing inefficiencies persist ("we're never hiding that from you", CEO, 2025 investor day).

External sources: ABB, Schneider and Vertiv all expanded margin in the quarter Eaton contracted, as above. Distributor-channel reporting shows Eaton's 2026 price increases running at industry-normal magnitude and on the same schedule as Hubbell's [web]. One independent analysis places Schneider, not Eaton, as the grid-to-chip integration benchmark Eaton is moving toward (electroneconomics.substack.com, accessed 2026-08-17) [web]. On the corroborating side, Microsoft's Americas President and CyrusOne appeared on video at the 2025 investor day endorsing the EnergyAware UPS and the data-centre partnership; those are curated customer testimonials and evidence that the relationships exist.

Ground-up view: the entry barrier here is qualification. Medium- and low-voltage switchgear must be type-tested to UL/ANSI or IEC standards, specified by a consulting engineer, accepted by the owner's standards group and serviced by a network the owner trusts. That takes years and reference installations. It does not take $20bn of revenue. Powell Industries, at $1,104m of FY2025 revenue with almost no goodwill, earned a 29.0% return on capital employed, a 19.7% operating margin and a 16.3% five-year revenue CAGR, and its latest-quarter operating margin of 20.6% is above Eaton's consolidated figure.▪ Minimum efficient scale binds at the plant and the engineering team; capacity in this industry is bought, and ABB, Schneider, GE Vernova and Vertiv are all buying it. Switching costs are asymmetric: high for the installed base, where replacing a switchgear lineup means an outage, a protection-scheme re-study and retraining, and low at a new build, where the specification is written by a third-party consulting engineer paid to keep two or three manufacturers biddable. Eaton's own description of its negotiation pipeline as "the aggregate value of orders in advanced commercial negotiation" describes a bid process. Buyer power is rising as the counterparty mix moves toward large direct accounts. Supplier power showed up as a cost: copper is available to every competitor at the same price, so the margin difference between Eaton, ABB and Schneider in Q2 2026 is a difference in what each recovered.

Basis. Operating income = net sales less cost of products sold, selling and administrative expense and research and development expense, because Eaton's income statement presents no operating-income subtotal. NOPAT = operating income × (1 − the year's effective tax rate). Capital employed = total assets less total current liabilities, two-year average. ROIC ex-intangibles removes goodwill and other intangible assets from capital employed. Section 13 uses a narrower invested-capital definition (debt plus equity less cash) and produces 15.9% for FY2025; both appear where used, and the difference is one of definition.

Incremental returns over the decade are exceptional and have a specific cause. Change in NOPAT over change in capital employed was 32.5% across 2016–2025 and 47.9% across 2020–2025, because growth was funded by selling capital-heavy low-return businesses. Lighting went to Signify in March 2020 and Hydraulics to Danfoss in August 2021, so NOPAT nearly doubled between 2019 and 2025 while net capital employed grew only $4.2bn despite $4.5bn spent on Tripp Lite and Cobham. That source is now spent: Mobility is the last low-return unit and it leaves in Q1 2027.

Versus peers. From each company's SEC XBRL filings, accessed 2026-08-17. Gross margins are not comparable across these filers because cost-of-revenue composition differs — Emerson, Rockwell and ITW push more cost into selling and administrative expense — so operating margin, capex and ROIC are the comparable measures.

Comparability flags: Hubbell's Q2 2026 was not yet tagged at extraction, so its latest quarter is one behind. nVent's +53% includes the Avail and EPG acquisitions and its FY2025 operating margin absorbs transaction and integration charges. GE Vernova separated from GE in April 2024, so no five-year CAGR is meaningful. Powell, Rockwell and Emerson report on September fiscal years and Parker on June, so their "latest quarter" is the three months to 31 March 2026.

Over time, the margin gaps have narrowed. Eaton Electrical stood 330 basis points above ABB Electrification in FY2024, 290 in FY2025 and 40 below in Q2 2026. Against Vertiv, whose consolidated adjusted operating margin was 4.9% in 2020 against Eaton Electrical's 18.5%, the gap closed to 190 basis points in Q2 2026. The 2020–2025 margin expansion was cohort-average: Eaton Electrical +790 basis points against Rockwell +860, Hubbell +730 and Parker's total segment margin +740 on their own consolidated results.▪ Reinvestment intensity moved the other way, from 2.2% of revenue in FY2020 to 3.3% in FY2025 and about 3.5% guided for 2026. What is not eroding is the operating return: 38.9% on tangible capital in FY2025 and 33.7% annualised in H1 2026, with backlog, orders and book-to-bill all improving sharply.

Placement: this advantage earns excess returns today and is defensible over the next several years, exposed to erosion as customers consolidate their buying, as rivals with equal engineering depth close the portfolio gap, and as the 800-volt DC architecture reopens specification decisions that were settled.▪

Business-model analogues. The shape is engineered electrical hardware specified into long-lived installations, sold through a two-step distributor network and increasingly direct, monetised again through a decades-long service and retrofit tail, with serial bolt-on acquisitions supplying new capability. Parker Hannifin is the closest match — engineered motion and flow components, distributor-heavy channel, installed-base aftermarket, a margin history built on serial acquisition (Clarcor, Meggitt), FY2025 operating margin 21.9% and ROIC 16.4%; it breaks on mix, because Parker's aftermarket share is higher and more contractual than anything Eaton discloses in Electrical and Parker has no end market as concentrated as data centres. Hubbell is the direct structural twin in North America on the same hardware, channel and bolt-on cadence at a 20.7% operating margin and 15.7% ROIC; it breaks on reach, with no global manufacturing, no white-space data-centre position and about a quarter of Eaton Electrical's revenue. Rockwell Automation matches on channel and specification lock at similar returns (20.4% operating margin, 18.1% ROIC) and breaks favourably for Rockwell: the Logix control platform is a software switching cost, and Brightlayer monitors equipment instead of running the process, so a customer can change it without changing the plant.

3.2 Aerospace

Eaton's Aerospace franchise holds a real and specific advantage and it is visible in the operating numbers: a 23.9% FY2025 segment operating margin, a 37.7% pre-tax return on the assets the segment employs, and a repeatable pattern of winning more content on each successor platform — 2–3x the F-16 on the F-35, 2–3x the KC-135 on the KC-46A, 2x the A330/A340 on the A350, more than 8x the Black Hawk on FLRAA▪. The mechanism is certification: content is designed onto a programme, qualified under the type certificate, then sold across the production run plus an aftermarket tail. The 10-K lists total cost of ownership, product and system performance, quality, design engineering and timely delivery as the methods of competition here, and lists price for Electrical, Vehicle and eMobility. Backlog of $5,164m at 30 June 2026, up 28% and 18% organic at a 1.2 book-to-bill, is what that position looks like in the order book.

The advantage has not produced excess returns for Eaton's shareholders. Eaton bought most of this franchise: Souriau-Sunbank $907m in December 2019, Cobham Mission Systems $2,800m in June 2021, Ultra PCS $1,529m in January 2026 — $5,236m of purchase price against a segment earning $1,013m of pre-amortisation operating profit in FY2025, with segment goodwill at $2,977m at 31 December 2025 against $941m at the end of 2018.▪ Putting that purchase price back into the capital base and charging the amortisation it generates against the segment gives roughly 9% to 12% after tax [estimate: segment identifiable assets $2,684m plus goodwill $2,977m plus net acquired intangibles of $1,165–1,457m straight-lined over 12–19 years, less $700–900m of estimated segment operating liabilities; NOPAT $645–745m], against a cost of capital estimated at 9–10% and a company ROIC of 15.9% on the §13 definition.

The growth record points the same way. Aerospace revenue grew from $2,335m in FY2018 to $4,249m in FY2025, up 82%; chaining the organic bridges Eaton discloses each year — +7%, −22%, −2%, +11%, +11%, +10%, +12% — gives about 24% of cumulative organic growth, a 3.1% annual rate, with the rest from Souriau, Cobham and currency.▪ Since the COVID trough the organic rate has been 10–12%, which is the rate of the aerospace cycle: Honeywell's Aerospace segment grew 15%, 11% and 12% organically in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and Woodward's Aerospace segment grew 14.7% and 14.0% in FY2024 and FY2025 with no acquisition in either year.

Management's account and the evidence disagree on pricing. The 2022 investor conference described the aftermarket as creating "predictable, high-margin revenue streams", and the aftermarket line has grown faster than OEM for three straight years — 18.4% against 9.3% in FY2025, 23.3% against 8.7% in H1 2026 — lifting aftermarket to 39.0% of segment sales. Honeywell attributes all of its 2026 aerospace growth to price ("higher organic sales of $128 million in Commercial Aviation Aftermarket driven by increased pricing", HON 10-Q Q2 2026). Eaton's own margin bridges show commodity and wage inflation as a 260 basis point drag in FY2025 and 300 in Q2 2026, offset by volume, mix and Ultra PCS, with no price line. Eaton's aftermarket growth is volume and mix.

Two facts limit the aerospace advantage. A quarter of the segment is industrial filtration and golf grips, $1,055m of FY2025 sales, which arrived from Hydraulics in the 2020 reorganisation. And the 2020 behaviour was that of an operationally geared components business: revenue declined 10.4%, operating profit declined 30.4%, a 70% decremental margin, and margin went from 24.0% to 18.6%. The 2020 deck had called that channel predictable.

Eaton's Aerospace margin moved 70 basis points in three years, from 23.2% in FY2022 to 23.9% in FY2025, and is 22.8% in the latest quarter.▪ Every gap in that table closed, and none closed because Eaton improved: Parker recovered from Meggitt integration, Woodward executed, Honeywell deteriorated. On the pre-amortisation basis that makes Parker comparable, Parker was 420 basis points ahead in FY2025 (28.1% against 23.9%). Eaton's own margin restated onto the amortisation-inclusive basis Parker, HEICO, Moog and Woodward report is roughly 20–21% [estimate: $2,711m of disclosed Aerospace acquisition intangibles straight-lined over 12–15 years, 370–460bp of 2026 revenue, applied to the 24.3–24.7% guide].

Placement: an advantage that earns its keep and is defensible over the next several years on certified positions already won, open to erosion, and not converted into returns above the cost of capital because Eaton paid the seller for it.

Business-model analogues. Parker Hannifin's Aerospace Systems is the closest — certified airframe and engine content assembled by acquisition, a 23.3% FY2025 reported segment margin and an 11.8% pre-tax return on the $12,218m of segment assets Parker discloses including goodwill; almost the same economics arrived at the same way, with the caveat that Parker's margin is struck after $300m of allocated amortisation and Eaton's is not. Curtiss-Wright is the second — certified niche content, serial bolt-ons, a 17.0% FY2025 aerospace segment margin — and it breaks on capital deployment, compounding free cash into buybacks instead of into escalating deal multiples. TransDigm does not fit: its 53.8% June-quarter segment EBITDA margin comes from sole-source aftermarket pricing that Eaton's chief executive explicitly disclaims. Woodward is the counterexample inside the same product space, having built its aerospace position organically and earning about 25% pre-tax on segment assets including goodwill.

3.3 Mobility

Mobility earns a small excess return on a narrow base. Returns are a few points above a plausible cost of capital, and the part of the business producing the premium is the aftermarket and the commercial-vehicle transmission and clutch installed base, roughly a quarter of revenue.▪ The rest — light-vehicle valvetrain, superchargers, fuel-vapour components and eMobility power electronics — competes on annual price-down terms against buyers far larger than it is.

Between FY2019 and FY2025 Eaton added $422m of identifiable assets and goodwill to Vehicle plus eMobility and segment operating profit went from $477m to $405m. Incremental capital earned nothing over six years, and the same holds for every start year from 2018. eMobility alone went from $141m of identifiable assets in 2019 to $743m in 2025 while recording cumulative operating losses of $88m across 2020–2025. Segment ROIC was roughly 9–12% [estimate: FY2025 segment operating profit taxed at 17–24% over identifiable assets plus $626m of segment goodwill, with and without a payables and accruals offset of 18–20% of assets] against a standalone cost of capital of about 8–10%.

Where an advantage exists it is platform qualification and a parts annuity, and it holds volume without holding price. Customers do not churn — a former Eaton leader described the business as one that "hardly gives an excuse for any customer to kick them out" while "getting new customers is tough" (Third Bridge, interview 2026-02-13) [web]. But the FY2025 margin bridge shows commodity and wage inflation costing 250 basis points against 190 basis points of operating efficiency with no price factor named, and across FY2021–FY2025 price appears as a positive twice, in FY2022 as inflationary recovery and in FY2023 as net price realization. When the price/cost gap opened in 2025 the response was to exit the business instead of repricing it: Q1 2026 organic sales declined 6% on "a deliberate action to fix the tail, exiting a low-margin North America light vehicle business."

In July 2017 Eaton sold half its heavy- and medium-duty automated transmission business to Cummins for $600m, forming Eaton Cummins Automated Transmission Technologies; management then told investors that as the market converted from manual to automated, "that revenue ends up showing up in the joint venture." Income from all equity-method associates was $8m in FY2025 against a $903m carrying value. And eMobility never reached profitability across seven reported years.

Whole-segment profitability is nonetheless well above the driveline group. Mobility's FY2025 EBITDA margin was 17.0% — $405m of segment profit plus $123m of segment depreciation on $3,109m of sales — against Dana's 6.5%, American Axle's 9.8% and BorgWarner's 8.8%, and 16 points behind Allison's 33.1%. Two external sources describe the aftermarket's own margin as strong. Neither Eaton nor Dana publishes it.

Placement: a business earning above its cost of capital today and defensible for now, with the defence coming from qualification cycles and parts. Two of its four historically strongest positions — automated transmissions and the North American light-vehicle tail — have been half-sold and exited. The external price confirms it: Dana agreed in June 2026 to take the segment at a $5.1bn enterprise value while committing to strip $250m of cost, 7.6% of its 2026 estimated sales.

Business-model analogues. Allison Transmission is the same shape done well — a commercial-vehicle drivetrain incumbent qualified onto vehicle platforms and monetised through a long parts and service tail — converting 60–80% share of its niche into a 48.6% gross margin, 29.2% operating margin and roughly 21% ROIC, where Mobility converts a comparable structural position into 13.0% and 9–12%, because only about a quarter of its revenue is in that structure. Dana and American Axle are the same shape done badly: long OEM relationships, no repricing power, FY2025 operating margins of 1.9% each. For the aftermarket quarter the closer reference is Donaldson — content designed onto an engine or machine and replaced for the life of the asset — which breaks on frequency, because a transmission or axle is rebuilt rarely where a filter is consumed continuously.

4. Competitive landscape and market sizing

4.1 Electrical

Eaton Electrical is the largest single reportable electrical franchise among the US-listed comparables and the second- or third-largest data-centre electrical business globally, behind Schneider Electric and roughly level with Vertiv.▪ It is not the scale leader in the two largest pools it competes in: in front-of-the-meter utility distribution it is smaller than both Hubbell Utility Solutions and GE Vernova Grid Solutions, and in data-centre revenue it is about half Schneider's size. Its Electrical revenue compounded 11.4% a year over FY2023–FY2025, roughly half the rate of Vertiv (22.1%), nVent (20.8%) and GE Vernova Electrification (23.0%) and about the same as ABB Electrification.▪

Four pools with different structures are inside one segment, and Eaton holds a position in each.

Pool Structure Who sets price
Low- and medium-voltage building and industrial distribution An oligopoly of five — Schneider, ABB, Siemens, Eaton, Legrand — plus regional players including Mitsubishi Electric, Hyundai and Chint Specification-driven: consulting engineers and EPCs specify by manufacturer; Systems price is set at the project bid and Products by published multiplier schedules
Data-centre electrical infrastructure (grey space) Concentrated among Schneider, Vertiv, Eaton, ABB, Legrand, Delta and Huawei, plus modular integrators Hyperscalers and multi-tenant developers negotiate directly and standardise designs across sites; lead time is the near-term clearing variable
Front-of-the-meter utility distribution and substation Fragmented across Hubbell, Eaton, GE Vernova, Schneider, Siemens Energy and S&C, plus transformer specialists Investor-owned utilities tender off approved-vendor lists; multi-year approval cycles limit entry and share shift alike
Data-centre liquid cooling New and unsettled: Vertiv, Boyd (now Eaton), Schneider with Motivair, nVent, CoolIT, Asetek, LiquidStack, Rittal, Stulz Chip and server OEM design-in decides the socket; the cold-plate specification follows NVIDIA and the ODMs

Market sizing, built from disclosure. The data-centre pool assembled from each player's own disclosure on an FY2025 basis: Schneider's Data Centers and Networks at 30% of €40.2bn is about $13.7bn; Eaton at 21% of $27,448m is $5,764m; ABB's AI data centres at 9% of $33.2bn is about $3.0bn; Legrand's datacenter at 26% of €9.5bn is about $2.8bn; nVent's Systems Protection infrastructure vertical is $1,299m; Vertiv's $10,230m is not split by end market. Adding Vertiv at even 70% data-centre gives roughly $33bn across the named western players before Delta, Huawei, Mitsubishi, Siemens and the private modular integrators. On that base Eaton's share is roughly 17–19%, Schneider's roughly 41% and Vertiv's roughly 22%.▪ Each denominator moves with the definition — Schneider bundles networks, Eaton bundles distributed IT, ABB counts only AI data centres — so these are indicative.

Eaton's own two disclosed data points size the same pool from the other direction and do not reconcile with its revenue. A 307 GW US backlog described as fifteen years of construction at 2025 build rates implies a 2025 US build of about 20.5 GW; at $3.4m of Eaton content per megawatt that is about $70bn of addressable content built in the US in 2025, against Eaton's global data-centre and distributed-IT revenue of $5,764m. That gives a capture rate of roughly 8–10% [estimate: $5.8bn over 20.5 GW at $3.4m/MW, with the numerator global and the denominator US-only, so the true figure is lower]. A second angle, measured against 2025 capacity additions instead of the announced pipeline, gives 14–17% including distributed IT [estimate: $5,764m over 10–12 GW of global additions at $3.4m/MW]. The two angles span 8% to 17%, and they differ because one measures announced pipeline and the other measures capacity added. Both say the same thing about the metric: $3.4m per megawatt is the full bill of materials Eaton can address on a site it wins in full.▪

Share direction. Across FY2023–FY2025, Eaton Electrical compounded 11.4%, ABB Electrification about 11% comparable in FY2025, GE Vernova Electrification 23.0%, Vertiv 22.1%, nVent 20.8%, Hubbell 4.3% and Schneider about 5.8% at group level. Eaton grows above the diversified incumbents and below the data-centre-concentrated players, which is what its mix implies: roughly 29% of Electrical is data centre against close to 100% for Vertiv.

Counter-evidence to the share claim, ranked by importance.

  • Every named competitor reports the same data-centre acceleration in the same quarter. ABB reported triple-digit data-centre order growth inside Electrification orders of $7,231m, up 58% comparable; Schneider reported triple-digit data-centre demand growth and raised FY2026 organic guidance to 10–13%; nVent's Systems Protection revenue rose 70%; Vertiv guides FY2026 organic growth to about 31%. If the underlying market grows 23% and five players each grow 50–100%, either the 23% is understated or share is moving from unlisted and Asian suppliers.▪
  • Vertiv is growing about twice as fast off a comparable base and now matches Eaton on margin. Its Americas segment operating margin was 27.6% in Q2 2026 against Eaton Electrical Americas' 27.5%, having been 24.0% against 29.5% a year earlier, a 560 basis point relative swing in four quarters.▪
  • Conversion capacity is Eaton's constraint, and competitors are adding capacity too. Vertiv guided FY2026 capex to about 4% of sales; ABB announced $200m across Europe in Q2 2026. Backlog that cannot be shipped is available to a competitor with capacity.
  • Inorganic entry is reshaping the utility and transformer pool. GE Vernova consolidated Prolec GE on 2 February 2026, taking Power Transmission from $759m to $1,877m in a single quarter; nVent bought Avail Infrastructure; Schneider bought Motivair. Eaton's counter-moves run the same direction, so the net effect is a faster-consolidating industry with a larger leader in the utility pool.
  • The 800-volt DC transition reopens the specification. Vertiv's Q2 2026 deck sets out three parallel 800-volt architectures with a named validation site and claims the world's first AI data centre adopting 800 VDC. Both companies claim the same lead in the same technology at the same time, and an architecture transition is the event that lets a specification-locked incumbent lose a socket.

Eaton is a mid-tier supplier in aerospace systems. Share direction. Ranked by six-year revenue CAGR of each player's aerospace line on its own fiscal calendar: HEICO 13.9%, Eaton 9.4%, TransDigm 9.1%, Moog 4.9%, Honeywell Aerospace 3.7%, Woodward Aerospace 3.5%. On the June 2026 quarter, ranked by reported revenue growth: HEICO +25%, TransDigm +22%, Woodward +19%, Moog +15%, Eaton +13%, Collins +8%, Honeywell Aerospace +5%. Only Eaton and Collins publish an organic bridge for the quarter, and Eaton's organic 7% is below every reported figure in that list. Where Eaton has taken content is visible in the OEM line: its OEM revenue compounded 10.2% over 2023–2025 against 5.0% for combined Airbus and Boeing deliveries and 2.4% for Honeywell's commercial aviation original equipment.

Counter-evidence, ranked by importance. Eaton's own 2026 guidance embeds no outgrowth: weighting its end-market bands gives blended aerospace market growth of roughly 8.4% [estimate: commercial aerospace at 9% of sales in the double-digit band and defence at 6% in the solid-growth band, at band midpoints] against an Aerospace organic guide of 7.5–9.5%. Its organic guide moved 7–9% to 7.5–9.5% while Electrical Americas moved 9–11% to 14–16%. Organic growth decelerated across three quarters, +10%, +9%, +7%, while combined Airbus and Boeing deliveries rose 25% in 2025. The "13-plus years of OE backlog" framing shrinks mechanically as the ramp happens: at end-2025 the Airbus and Boeing order books were 8,748 and 6,713 units against deliveries of 793 and 600, which is 11.0 and 11.2 years [web]. And the aftermarket faces parts-manufacturer-approval competition: HEICO's Flight Support Group, which the company describes as designing and manufacturing FAA-approved replacement parts "for sale at lower prices than those manufactured by OEMs", reached $3,117m in fiscal 2025, 73% the size of Eaton's whole Aerospace segment, and rose from 60% of HEICO net sales in fiscal 2023 to 70% in fiscal 2025.

Eaton is not the scale leader in any Mobility business line. Its $3,109m of FY2025 revenue is roughly 40% of Dana's $7,500m of continuing-operations sales and 22% of BorgWarner's $14,316m, and eMobility is about a quarter the size of BorgWarner's PowerDrive Systems, which grew 21% in 2025 while eMobility declined 9%.▪ Allison Transmission, at $3,010m, is the closest revenue-scale peer and earns a 29.2% operating margin on the fully-automatic transmission niche Eaton does not serve.

Where the structure has moved against Eaton is vertical integration. Three of PACCAR's four named North American truck competitors now sell an in-house automated transmission — Daimler's Detroit DT12, PACCAR's TX-12, Volvo's I-Shift, which took 94% of Volvo Group's own North American orders as of 2021 [web].▪ Eaton's own Vehicle sector head called vertical integration "largely behind us" in February 2016. And the growing, value-dense product line left the segment in 2017: Eaton Cummins Automated Transmission Technologies is equity-accounted, so its revenue never appears in Mobility, and it announced its 500,000th Endurant transmission in August 2025 [web].

The equipment layer where Eaton operates captures about 5% of each data-centre dollar and the compute layer captures most of the rest.▪ The two layers immediately adjacent to Eaton — the interconnect supplier above and the distributor below — both widened gross margin in the twelve months to mid-2026 while Eaton's narrowed. Eaton is not disclosed as a customer or supplier of any company named here; the 10-K states raw materials are purchased from many suppliers and names none, and customer concentration appears only as unnamed groups.

The binding constraint moves with the horizon. For the next four to six quarters it is inside Eaton's factories: firm backlog reached $24.1bn at 30 June 2026 from $19.8bn at 31 December 2025, 71% of it targeted for delivery inside twelve months, with Electrical Americas book-to-bill at 1.3 and trailing organic orders up 41%.▪ The CEO frames it the same way: "Scaling capacity to turn demand into revenue remains the clear priority in the business." Revenue per day rose about 25% from the start of 2025. Against that description, Eaton's own capital spending is measured: $757m, $808m and $919m in FY2023–FY2025, 3.2–3.3% of sales, and $446m in H1 2026 against $11,079m paid for acquisitions in the same six months. The "more than $1 billion" capacity programme is multi-year.

From 2028, when management says the majority of the 307 GW converts, the constraint moves upstream of Eaton to grid interconnection and permitting. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's 2026 survey puts more than 2,060 GW of generation and storage actively seeking US grid interconnection at end-2025, with a median duration above five years for projects that came online in 2025 [web]. Dell'Oro's research director states that access to power is the defining challenge for the buildout [web]. Equinix describes the same constraint from the buyer's side and puts money behind it: its FY2025 10-K says supply-chain challenges "have driven us to invest in and commit to future purchases in advance of our standard practice", with total future purchase commitments of $8,411m at 31 December 2025 against FY2025 revenue of $9,217m. Eaton controls neither queue and cannot relieve either with capital.

Lead times are contested inside Eaton's own record. The CEO said in December 2025 that "over time, we improved our lead times... we are reducing lead times" and used that to argue rising backlog is demand and not queueing; in July 2026 he said "we know the product lines where our lead times are extended." Trade sources put data-centre-specification medium-voltage switchgear at two to three years and substation transformers at 100 to 150 weeks in 2026 [web]. Eaton publishes no lead-time series.

Supplier interface. Freeport-McMoRan's consolidated realised copper price was $6.04/lb in H1 2026 against $4.48/lb in H1 2025, up 34.8%, and COMEX copper set a record $6.77/lb intraday on 7 August 2026 [web]. A 50% Section 232 tariff on the full customs value of semi-finished copper products and 25% on copper-intensive derivative products took effect on 6 April 2026, with ores, concentrates, cathodes, anodes and scrap excluded [web]. Electrical Americas absorbed 470 basis points of commodity inflation in both Q2 and H1 2026, about $355m of incremental input cost in six months. Eaton's disclosed commodity hedge sensitivity to a 10% price move is under $1m; Vertiv's is $15.8m on roughly 37% of Eaton's revenue. Eaton's response is price and payment terms: supply-chain finance obligations inside accounts payable rose from $369m at 1 January 2024 to $669m at 30 June 2026, with $1,126m of invoices confirmed in H1 2026 alone and days payable at about 94.

The copper increase was captured one layer up: Freeport widened gross profit per pound from $1.72 to $2.00 in FY2025. Cleveland-Cliffs did not: the sole US producer of grain-oriented electrical steel ran a −5% Steelmaking gross margin in FY2025 and 2% in Q2 2026 while its average selling price rose from $1,015 to $1,124 per net ton. Amphenol did, at 36.9% against 33.8%.

Distributor interface. WESCO's FY2025 10-K describes the other side: more than 35,000 suppliers, the ten largest about 32% of purchases and no single supplier above 6%; most supplier agreements terminable by either party on 60 days' notice or less; and supplier volume rebate income of 1.4% of net sales in 2025, about $328m recorded as a reduction of cost of goods sold. Over the twelve months to June 2026 WESCO's gross margin rose to 21.8% from 21.1% while Eaton's consolidated gross margin declined to 33.5% from 37.0%. The distributor passed the commodity increase through and kept some.▪

Customer interface. NVIDIA published the 800-volt DC ecosystem on 13 October 2025 and named nine qualified data-centre power-systems partners, Eaton among them. Its own claims for the architecture are that "with 800 VDC, the same wire gauge can carry 157% more power than 415 VAC", that redundant conversion stages are eliminated, and that the Kyber rack converter "occupies 26% less area than traditional multi-stage approaches" [web]. Each of those reduces the physical content per megawatt of the layer Eaton sells, while the CEO states content per megawatt holds at $3.4m through the transition. Eaton's case has to be that it wins a larger share of a smaller physical bill of materials, or that solid-state transformers and cooling add more value than the conversion stages remove.▪

The customer has also stopped pre-committing. The CEO at UBS on 2 December 2025: "Q1 '24, we had a multiyear order, which was above $1 billion from a particular customer. We see less of these multiyear orders because... the customers believe that we can deliver because we invest in capacity... with the chips changing every 18 to 2 years, customers would not love to place orders 3, 4 years out when technology might change." In the same answer he described the substitution: "we're substituting this big order with the new bread-and-butter business... we negotiate orders around $500 million, $600 million, $700 million. They're much more frequent."

Customer economics. Capital spending by three implied end customers went from $126,324m in H1 2025 to $228,122m in H1 2026, up 81%, and Dell'Oro puts the top four US hyperscalers near $600bn combined for 2026 [web]. Eaton's H1 2026 data-centre revenue against $228bn of half-year spending by three buyers is under two cents per dollar. The asset-life mismatch runs against the buyer: Meta sets five to 5.5 years for servers and network assets and 25 to 30 years for buildings, and Amazon changed the estimated useful lives of a subset of servers and networking equipment effective 1 January 2025 after an earlier change effective 1 January 2024. Eaton's exposure is the order rate. Equipment shipped is paid for regardless of what the compute earns, with no vendor financing and no equity in any customer, and a pause in the site decision stops orders immediately while the backlog and the twelve ramping factories keep running.

Circularity. Eaton takes no equity in customers, extends no vendor financing and guarantees no customer obligations. Its equity-method positions are supply- and channel-side: 49% of NordicEPOD, which assembles standardised power modules for Nordic data centres, and a stake in Jiangsu Ryan Electrical, a Chinese distribution and sub-transmission transformer maker. The only residual value guarantee disclosed relates to a synthetic lease on an Eaton facility.

The aerospace profit pool concentrates one layer along: TransDigm's gross margin excluding depreciation was 61.3% in its June 2026 quarter.

6.2 Growth attribution: did the claimed driver show up

Against Eaton's own ultimate volume driver. Revenue is booked when equipment ships against construction in progress, not when a project is announced. Each link in that chain has its own measured rate.

Link Series Growth Source
Announcements Eaton's own account of 2025 industry announcements "up over 200% year-over-year" Q4 2025 call
Construction starts US data-centre construction starts, $26.9bn (2024) → $77.7bn (2025) +189% ConstructConnect [web]
