The rate declines at every step from announcement toward physical completion. Eaton's revenue is generated nearest the put-in-place step, which grew 46%. Measured there, Eaton's 65% is about 19 points of outgrowth; measured against the 23% market figure management uses on the call, it is 42.▪

Against industry dollars and a peer cohort. In the June 2026 quarter, sorted by electrical-segment organic revenue growth: nVent +47%, GE Vernova Electrification +29% organic, ABB Electrification +19% comparable, Eaton Electrical +18%, Schneider Energy Management +18%, Hubbell Electrical Solutions +18%, Vertiv +18% organic, and Legrand +9.8% for H1. On disclosed data-centre growth: nVent guides data-centre sales to about $2bn in 2026, more than double 2025; Hubbell reported data-centre sales +65%; GE Vernova booked more than $5bn of data-centre orders year to date, more than double FY2025; Eaton +65% organic. Eaton's Electrical organic growth is the cohort median and its data-centre growth matches Hubbell's and trails nVent's and GE Vernova's.

The secular driver in the realised numbers. It appeared, and it accounts for the whole of the outgrowth against Eaton's own plan. The March 2022 investor conference planned Electrical from an $11.1bn 2020 base to $16.5bn by 2025 at an 8.2% CAGR; realised was $20,091m at 12.6%.▪ Splitting the $3.6bn beat: data centres and distributed IT were planned at 23% of the 2025 mix, about $3.80bn, and realised $5,764m, so $1.96bn or 55% of the beat is that one market. The remaining 45% came from the rest of Electrical compounding about 9.2% against a plan near 6.7%, and a material part of that was 2021–2022 pricing, which the CEO says will not repeat: "it's not stepping up in the model. We see it normalizing. So most of the growth will be from volume." Over the same plan the industrial businesses undershot: Aerospace, Vehicle and eMobility were planned at $8.3bn including acquisitions by 2025 and realised $7,358m, with eMobility planned at roughly $980m organic and realised at $604m with an operating loss.

Two markets contributed almost nothing. Industrial facilities, 11% of company sales and 15% of Electrical, was named as an offset to organic growth in FY2024, FY2025, Q1 2026 and H1 2026, and on the disclosed mix went from about $3.0bn to about $3.0bn. Utility, 11% of sales, produced order growth in the double digits on a trailing basis while the H1 2026 10-Q names it as a drag on Electrical Americas organic revenue, which is the order-to-revenue lag in utility distribution behaving as management describes it, against US investor-owned utility capital expenditure rising 17% in 2026 to $238.8bn with distribution about a third of the total [web].

6.3 Three tests of the share claim

Test A — the company-level arithmetic. Eaton's own blended 2026 end-market growth estimate moved from about 7% (Q4 2025 deck) to about 10% (Q2 2026 deck) while the FY2026 organic guide moved from 7–9% to 11–13%. Company-level outgrowth therefore went from about 1 point at the earlier pair to about 2 points at the later one. Data centres and distributed IT at 21% of the base, growing 65% against a 23% market, would alone contribute 8.8 points of company outgrowth. The other 79% of the portfolio would have to undergrow its markets by about 8.6 points for both to hold.

Test B — solve the segment guides. The FY2026 segment guides imply Electrical organic growth of 14.0% (0.484 × 15% + 0.248 × 12%, over 0.732). Data centres and distributed IT are 28.7% of Electrical. Solving for the two components:

If the rest of Electrical grows Implied FY2026 data-centre and distributed-IT organic growth
0% 48.8%
5% 36.4%
7% 31.4%
and if data centres hold 65% the rest of Electrical contracts 6.5%

Eaton's own guidance is consistent with full-year data-centre and distributed-IT growth of roughly 31–37% if the rest of Electrical grows 5–7%, against the 65% quarterly rate management highlights. It is not consistent with 65% data centres and broad-based double-digit growth elsewhere.▪

Test C — the capture rate inside the per-megawatt unit. Eaton's 2025 data-centre and distributed-IT revenue was $5,764m. US data-centre power demand rose about 6 GW in 2025 and global additions are roughly twice the US, so approximately 10–12 GW [estimate: US net addition doubled for the rest of the world; bounds 9–14 GW]. At $3.4m per megawatt the accessible content on 2025 additions was $34–41bn, so Eaton's revenue is 14–17% of it, and that numerator includes distributed IT, which is not new-build capacity. The second angle in §4.1, against the pipeline-implied US build of 20.5 GW, gives 8–10%. The two span 8% to 17%.

Applying the middle of that range to the headline pipeline: 307 GW × $3.4m/MW is $1,044bn of accessible content, which at a 10–15% capture spread over the fifteen years management assigns it comes to roughly $7–10bn a year of US data-centre revenue [estimate: pipeline × content per MW × capture range ÷ 15 years]. That supports growth and it implies compounding in the high single digits to low teens over the horizon, against the 30–65% rates the recent quarters print.

6.4 The per-megawatt unit, and what it measures

Date Source Figure Label used
Oct 2023 Q3 2023 call ~$1.5m/MW "Eaton's market opportunity in data centers"
11 Mar 2025 Investor day, slide 67 $1.2–1.5m traditional; $1.2–2.9m AI; 6–14% of total compute and infrastructure capex "Eaton potential sales per MW"
Oct 2025 Q3 2025 call $1.2–2.4m today, plus $0.5m from Boyd range, cloud at the low end
3 Feb 2026 Q4 2025 call $2.9m today, $3.4m after Boyd "dollars per megawatt of accessible market"
31 Jul 2026 Q2 2026 call $3.4m "the right number to think about it. So for your modeling, it is the right one"

The figure changed in three ways:

  • Restated before Boyd: $2.4m in October 2025 and $2.9m in February 2026 from the same executive, one quarter apart, with the bridge given at the UBS conference in December 2025 and not on either call.
  • Partly purchased: about $0.5m of the $3.4m, roughly 15%, arrived with Boyd in March 2026.
  • Range to point: a bounded range with an explicit architecture caveat, "not every data center is going to require it", became a single point offered as a modelling input.▪

The deck's own capex anchor gives a different answer: at 6–14% of a site's total compute and infrastructure capex, $3.4m per megawatt implies total build capex of $24–57m per megawatt, against the $20–29m the deck's own range implies.

6.5 Internal consistency of the pipeline metrics

The US data-centre backlog series went 206 GW at eleven years of build (Q4 2025 call), 228 GW at twelve years (Q1 2026), 307 GW at fifteen years (Q2 2026) — a 49% increase in two quarters, with implied 2025 US build rates of 18.7, 19.0 and 20.5 GW. On the same Q2 2026 call the CEO described "the 50 gigawatts that was built over decades that's going to be online by the end of this year", and at the UBS conference in December 2025 he put US data-centre capacity at around 20 GW. A 20.5 GW annual build against a 50 GW cumulative base means 41% of everything ever built went in during 2025. The external series does not support that rate: US data-centre power demand went from about 25 GW to 31 GW in 2025 with 41 GW forecast for 2026, a net addition nearer 6–10 GW, and independent measurement puts US capacity commissioned in 2025 at 8.5 GW. On the observed build rate the 307 GW pipeline is thirty to fifty years of backlog. Two figures management gave on the same call cannot both describe the same quantity.▪

The negotiation pipeline turned. Q1 2026: "our negotiations pipeline was up 81% in Q1 over prior year." Q2 2026: "our negotiations pipeline was up 60% year-to-date over prior year." The basis changed from a quarterly to a year-to-date comparison in the same quarter the headline declined 21 points; if the two bases were comparable and the quarterly values similar, the Q2 standalone rate would be roughly 39% [estimate: 2 × 1.60 − 1.81]. This is the earliest-turning number Eaton discloses. Sequential backlog additions moved the same way: Electrical Americas added $1,213m in Q1 2026 and $716m in Q2, down 41%, while trailing-twelve-month organic order growth was flat at 42% then 41%.

6.6 Cyclical against secular

Year Revenue $m Note
2014 22,552 prior peak
2016 19,747 trough, −12.4% from 2014
2019 21,390 peak; includes Lighting and Hydraulics
2020 17,858 trough; Lighting divested March 2020
2025 27,448 Hydraulics divested 2021

Peak to peak, 2014 to 2025 is 1.8% a year on a portfolio that lost Lighting (about $1.7bn) and Hydraulics (about $2.2bn) and gained Tripp Lite, Cobham, Royal Power, Fibrebond, Exertherm, Ultra PCS and Boyd. The CEO's own framing: 112 years to reach $20bn of revenue through Cooper, then "the following decade... we just grew $1 billion the top line." On a comparable Electrical perimeter, 2019 Electrical less Lighting of about $11.7bn against $20,091m in 2025 is about 9.4% a year across six years including a pandemic trough.

The current position is a late-expansion capacity build. Firm backlog across the three growth segments was $23,941m at 30 June 2026 against $30,026m of trailing revenue, 9.6 months of shipments; twenty-four Electrical Americas facility expansions are in flight, twelve ramping and twelve to come; capital intensity peaks in 2026 on the CFO's guidance; and commodity inflation took 470 basis points off Electrical Americas margin in H1 2026 and about 390 basis points off consolidated gross margin. Q1 2026 showed the leverage in reverse: Electrical Americas margin declined 440 basis points year over year to 25.6% when volume arrived a quarter behind the cost.

6.7 Technology and policy shifts that change the slope

The 800-volt DC architecture removes conversion stages between the utility feed and the rack, which is unit count Eaton currently supplies, and adds solid-state transformers and DC breakers it does not yet ship in volume. First orders are guided to H2 2026 and shipments to late 2027. The second-order effect is on the source of advantage: a solid-state transformer's cost is silicon-carbide devices and controls, which is a different capability from copper-and-steel fabrication scale, distribution and field service. Modularisation moves value from site-built assemblies to factory-built power blocks, favours scale suppliers, and standardises the deliverable so a customer's second source is easier to qualify. Liquid cooling is a design-win business that resets with each chip generation, so Boyd's position must be re-won on Rubin and its successors. Behind-the-meter generation, through the Siemens Energy partnership, raises medium-voltage switchgear and paralleling content and loosens the interconnection constraint.

On policy, grid interconnection gates when the 307 GW converts and Eaton controls none of it. Copper passes through with a lag and the pricing actions were implemented in Q2 and early August 2026. Tariff exposure in the realised numbers is small — the Q2 2026 IEEPA refund impact was under $3m, "$2.8 million, if you want to be precise." The effective tax rate moved from 17.6% in H1 2025 to 24.9% in H1 2026 and 28.1% in Q2 2026 alone, on more income in higher-tax jurisdictions plus withholding tax on funding Boyd, and cost $0.15 of Q2 EPS against a $0.25 segment-profit beat.

6.8 What turns first

Ordered by lead time, longest first: negotiation-pipeline growth, which appears only on the calls and has already decelerated; quarterly customer orders as given on the call, distinct from the trailing figure in the 10-Q; sequential backlog additions, derivable from the 10-Q; trailing-twelve-month organic order change, which lags an inflection two to three quarters; and book-to-bill, a four-quarter average, which lags most. Commercial and institutional left the Electrical Americas organic-growth attribution sentence in the 10-Q between Q1 and Q2 2026 while the CEO described it growing double digits on the same day's call.

7. Critical points

1. The near-term revenue path is set by throughput. Electrical Americas backlog reached $15,175m at 30 June 2026, 1.05x trailing segment revenue against 0.78x at the end of 2023, with trailing organic orders up 41% and book-to-bill at 1.3. Revenue per shipping day rose about 25% between Q1 2025 and Q2 2026 while backlog rose 51% over the same stretch. Eaton is spending more than $1bn across twenty-four capacity projects to close it, and its FY2026 Electrical Americas guide of 14–16% organic implies H2 revenue of roughly $3.9bn a quarter against Q2's $3,951m, flat sequentially, which an analyst put to management on the Q2 call without being disputed.

2. Margin, not demand, is the live question, and the guided repair is large. Electrical Americas margin went 30.2% (FY2024), 29.9% (FY2025), 25.6% (Q1 2026), 27.5% (Q2 2026), with a 470 basis point commodity drag in both Q2 and H1. The FY2026 guide of 28.8–29.2% needs H2 near 31.2%, a 450–500 basis point step of which the CFO attributes 300 basis points to price/cost and 150–200 to output and productivity. The comparable 2025 step was about 40 basis points.▪ The segment printed above 30% in three of the last eight quarters and peaked at 31.6% in Q4 2024, and the guided Q4 2026 exit rate of 32.0–32.5% equals the 2030 target four years early.

3. GAAP earnings are declining while revenue accelerates, and the cause is the balance sheet. Q2 2026 revenue grew 21% and GAAP diluted EPS declined 16% to $2.11; H1 revenue grew 19% and GAAP EPS declined 13%. Intangible amortisation doubled to $255m in the quarter from $129m, net interest nearly tripled to $201m from $71m, and the effective tax rate went from 17.2% to 28.1%. FY2026 guidance is GAAP $10.36–$10.56 against FY2025's $10.45 actual, and adjusted $13.40–$13.60. Roughly $1.2bn of annual cost is outside the number the annual bonus is paid on.

4. Eaton spent more on acquisitions in six months than in the prior seven years combined, and the return starts low. Cash paid for acquisitions was $11,079m in H1 2026 against $8,029m across 2019–2025. Boyd Thermal cost $9,549m and generates roughly $415m of segment operating profit at its guided $1.8bn of revenue and realised 23.1% margin, about 3.3% after tax on the price paid against an estimated 8–10% cost of capital, before any amortisation of the $7,190m of intangibles the deal created. Company return on capital employed moves from 13.8% in FY2025 to roughly 10–11% on the post-Boyd base even at restored FY2025 operating margins.

5. The content-per-megawatt unit is an addressable pool and it is being used as a revenue multiplier. The March 2025 deck defines $1.2–2.9m per megawatt for AI sites as "potential sales per MW" and 6–14% of a site's total capex; the Q4 2025 call defines $3.4m as "accessible market" per megawatt; the Q2 2026 call endorses $3.4m as a modelling input. Realised revenue per global megawatt commissioned is $0.21–0.32m, and capture against the accessible pool is 8–17% depending on the denominator. A model that multiplies gigawatts by $3.4m computes the addressable pool.

6. Two markets produced most of Electrical's growth, so the breadth claim describes the base. Data centres accounted for roughly 60% of Electrical's FY2025 revenue increase of $2,407m and commercial and institutional roughly a quarter, together about 85%. Industrial facilities, 15% of Electrical revenue, contributed roughly 1%.▪ Residential and light vehicle are at cyclical lows.

7. The margin story in Electrical is one region. Electrical Americas added 970 basis points of margin between 2020 and 2025; Electrical Global went from 15.9% to 19.4% and has been between 18.4% and 19.4% in every year since 2021 at 34% of Electrical revenue. The 2030 plan requires Electrical to reach about 30%; if Global holds near 19.5%, Americas has to reach roughly 35%, against its own 32% target and a record annual high of 30.2%.▪

8. Leverage moved a decade's worth in six months and there is no covenant to stop it. Total debt went from $9,895m to $20,611m and net debt from $9,092m to $19,916m. Net debt to EBITDA moved from 1.47x at FY2025 to 3.09x on trailing EBITDA and about 2.9x pro-forma for full-year Boyd and Ultra PCS, against a 1.26–2.57x band across the prior ten years. Interest cover went from 21.5x for FY2025 to 6.7x on Q2 2026. Eaton has no financial maintenance covenant, publishes no leverage target and no deleveraging schedule, and no post-Boyd rating action appears in any archived filing.

9. Mobility leaves in Q1 2027 and the arithmetic of what Eaton receives is contested. Enterprise value $5.1bn, roughly $1.1bn of cash to Eaton, Eaton shareholders taking at least 50.1% of the combined Dana. Dana's stated 8.3x pre-synergy multiple assumes $614m of 2026 estimated EBITDA against Eaton's FY2025 reported segment EBITDA of $528m; on Eaton's own figure the price is 9.7x unsynergised and 6.6x fully synergised. The $250m synergy commitment equals 7.6% of Mobility's 2026 estimated sales and 62% of its FY2025 segment operating profit, is underwritten by Dana, and accrues to a company Eaton shareholders will own just over half of.

10. The one point-in-time leading indicator was reduced to an annual update. Through Q4 2024 every earnings call included a megaproject tracker with project count, cumulative value, start rate, win rate and a cancellation rate, last given on a call as "around 10% and well below historical levels" in Q3 2024. "Cancellation" appears seven times on the Q3 2024 call, four on Q4 2024, once on Q1 2025 and zero across the five calls since; "win rate" last appeared in Q3 2025. On the Q4 2025 call management said the megaproject update would move to an annual cadence. Backlog counts firm orders only and Eaton states a significant portion of open orders are not firm; book-to-bill is a four-quarter average and order growth is trailing twelve months.

8. Management claim pressure tests

"$3.4 million per megawatt is the right number for your modeling." The March 2025 deck defines the figure as Eaton potential sales per megawatt within a $1.2–2.9m range for AI sites and $1.2–1.5m for traditional, and anchors it at 6–14% of a site's total compute and infrastructure capex. The Q4 2025 call defines $3.4m as accessible market per megawatt. Applying it to Eaton's own stated near-term conversion of about 61 GW, 20% of the 307 GW pipeline, produces $207bn of revenue against Electrical's FY2025 revenue of $20,091m and its own 2030 organic target of $31bn-plus. Realised revenue per megawatt of global capacity commissioned is $0.21–0.32m [estimate: FY2025 data-centre revenue of $4.6–4.9bn over 14–15 GW of 2025 global additions or 23 GW of 2026 scheduled additions], so Eaton realises 6–11% of the stated potential. The figure measures addressable content.

"Much, much faster than the underlying market that is growing at 23%. So definitely gaining momentum, gaining share." The 23% denominator is management's own, undefined and unsourced, and it declined from "around the low 30s" at Q2 2025 while Eaton's reported growth accelerated from 50% to 65%, so the claimed outgrowth widened from about 20 points to about 42 in a year. Measured against US private data-centre construction put in place, which grew 46% year over year in April 2026, the outgrowth is about 19 points. In the same quarter ABB reported triple-digit data-centre order growth, Schneider triple-digit demand growth, nVent 70% segment revenue growth and GE Vernova more than $5bn of data-centre orders year to date. An independent view attributes Eaton's gain to absorbing demand that sub-scale suppliers cannot serve at the required lead time, with Eaton's portfolio stopping at the server-hall boundary where Schneider and Vertiv extend into rack-level distribution and cooling (electroneconomics.substack.com, accessed 2026-08-17) [web]. The two explanations imply different persistence.

"307 gigawatts or 15 years of backlog at 2025 build rates." That ratio implies a 2025 US build of 20.5 GW. On the same call the CEO described "the 50 gigawatts that was built over decades" coming online by the end of 2026, and in December 2025 he put US capacity at around 20 GW. Independent measurement puts 2025 US commissioned capacity at 8.5 GW and net power-demand addition at about 6 GW [web]. On the observed rate the pipeline is thirty to fifty years of backlog. The pipeline itself grew 49% in two quarters, from 206 GW to 228 GW to 307 GW.

"The majority of the margin decline was driven by temporary negative price/cost." The lag is a property of the order book and the order book is growing. Systems is 71–76% of Electrical Americas revenue, priced at order and shipped months later; backlog coverage went from 0.78x annual revenue at the end of 2023 to about 1.05x at 30 June 2026, and 29% of company backlog is scheduled beyond twelve months. Direct commodity input runs 18–21% of segment revenue [estimate: two inversions of the disclosed margin bridges against published copper prices] and copper rose about 37% year over year in H1 2026, so a 22–28% blended basket move against a 20% intensity is 440–560 basis points of gross cost against the 470 basis points of net drag reported. The precedent one layer along is Vertiv in 2022: revenue grew 13.9% from $4,998m to $5,692m while operating profit declined 14% from $259.9m to $223.4m and operating margin went 5.2% to 3.9%, and operating margin reached 12.7% only in FY2023. Eaton is guiding full recovery inside two quarters.

"We are clearly ahead in terms of technology after the acquisition of Resilient Power last year." Eaton's three-year organic solid-state transformer programme was, on the CEO's own account at UBS on 2 December 2025, behind a startup Eaton then bought for $86m — $55m of cash at closing plus contingent consideration running to 2028. NVIDIA names nine qualified data-centre power-systems partners for 800-volt DC. On shipping dates, Vertiv's 800-volt DC ecosystem is reported commercially available in H2 2026 against Eaton shipments from late 2027 [web]. On the adjacent DC-breaker block, ABB's SACE Infinitus is described in ABB's own materials as fully IEC 60947-2 certified up to 2,500 A with a breaking time under 25 microseconds, while Eaton's medium-voltage hybrid breaker is an ARPA-E research programme [web].

"They are the market leaders for liquid cooling, if you think about the cold plates and the CDUs." TrendForce names four cold-plate suppliers — Cooler Master, AVC, Boyd and Auras — and reports sidecar coolant distribution units, the larger half of that market, led by Delta, with in-row units supplied primarily by Vertiv and Boyd [web]. At Eaton's own Barclays appearance the host raised reported Boyd share loss on Google's TPU v7 to an Asian competitor, and the answer did not address the programme. Eaton paid $9,549m, of which $196m is property, plant and equipment.

"Eaton is performing well in terms of margin versus their peers" (on Vehicle, March 2025). The claim is correct against the driveline group and wrong against the closest comparable in the same product category. Mobility's FY2025 EBITDA margin of 17.0% is roughly double Dana's 6.5%, American Axle's 9.8% and BorgWarner's 8.8%, on a revenue base one-half to one-quarter their size. Against Allison Transmission, which converts a comparable commercial-vehicle drivetrain incumbency into a 33.1% EBITDA margin and roughly 21% ROIC, Mobility runs 16 points behind on margin and roughly 9–12 points behind on returns.▪ Ten months after that statement Eaton announced the separation.

"No change. Same rigor" on the acquisition filter (CFO, March 2025). The stated floor moved. In 2018 and 2019 the CFO and CEO both described "a minimum of 300 basis points over our cost of capital" on an 8–9% cost of capital, with Souriau underwritten as accretive in year one. The March 2025 investor day states "EPS accretion within 2 years and having a return which is 2 to 3 points above our cost of capital", and the 2020 deck's "target minimum returns of 300 bps above cost of capital" became "target return of 200–300 bps" in the 2025 deck. On $9,549m of Boyd consideration the difference between a 200 and a 300 basis point spread is roughly $95m of annual economic profit. The accretion test is also written in adjusted EPS, which adds back the amortisation of the $7,190m of intangibles the deal created.

"We are committed to overachieving as a team. There is upside to the plan" (Q4 2025), alongside "it's too early to provide new targets for 2030." The March 2025 plan was built on five segments with Mobility inside and no inorganic contribution assumed. Two of its five segment margin targets apply to businesses leaving in Q1 2027, and removing Mobility raises the FY2025 company segment margin from 24.5% to 25.9% on mix alone [estimate: FY2025 segment sales of $24,340m and segment profit of $6,308m excluding Vehicle and eMobility], so the 28% target is mechanically easier than when it was set. From an ex-Mobility FY2025 base of $24,339m the $38bn 2030 revenue target requires 9.3% a year, above the top of Eaton's own 6–9% band. Management reaffirmed "our 2026 and 2030 commitments" on 31 July 2026, seven weeks after signing the Dana agreements, and cancelled the 2026 investor day.

"We plan to keep our share count flat" while the guide implies GAAP EPS is roughly flat. Working forward from management's own inputs — revenue near $32.7bn, the 24.3% segment-margin guide midpoint, the $1,450m corporate-expense guide, FY2026 amortisation of $911m built from the Q1 and Q2 actuals, and net interest of $715m built from the H1 actual plus the Q2 run-rate — pre-tax income comes to about $4,865m. The GAAP EPS guide midpoint of $10.46 on 389.4m shares needs $4,073m of net income and therefore a 16.3% full-year GAAP tax rate, against 24.9% realised in H1, which implies an 8.8% H2 rate. Closing the gap through profit instead needs a 25.4% full-year segment margin, a point above the top of the guide. Eaton printed GAAP EPS below its guided range in both Q1 and Q2 2026, the only range misses on either EPS measure across twenty-two quarters.

"Mobility will be the leading independent provider of engineered solutions to global vehicle, auto and off-highway OEMs" (Q4 2025), and the separation aligns capital "to the highest-return, highest-growth opportunities" (Q2 2026). Both are Eaton, six months apart. Dana's own diligence points the same way as the second statement: its CFO said "there's a lot more synergies on the purchasing side with Dana than there was actually in the broad umbrella of Eaton", its chairman said "our overhead cost structure is a lot leaner than Eaton's", and both described neglected automation capital. Eaton's capital behaviour preceded the words: Mobility capex was 1.5x segment depreciation in 2023, 0.84x in 2025 and 0.71x in H1 2026, while Electrical Americas ran 3.1x in 2025.

9. History and inflection points

Date Event Why it mattered
30 Nov 2012 Cooper Industries acquired for $13,192m; Eaton Corporation plc becomes the Irish-domiciled parent Total assets went from $17,873m to $35,491m, goodwill from $5,537m to $14,495m, long-term debt from $3,366m to $8,969m and weighted-average diluted shares from 343m to 477m. Eaton became majority-Electrical, which is what made the 2020s data-centre cycle relevant to it
Apr 2016 Craig Arnold becomes Chairman and CEO; asked whether the end of the post-inversion window brings a break-up, answers "I don't want to anyone sitting around thinking... we're going to announce some big transaction" Over the next five years he removed roughly a quarter of the revenue base
31 Jul 2017 50% of the heavy- and medium-duty automated transmission business sold to Cummins for $600m; $1,077m pre-tax gain, of which $544m from remeasuring the retained half The growing, value-dense commercial-vehicle product line moved into an equity-accounted joint venture and off Eaton's revenue line
2 Mar 2020 Lighting sold to Signify for $1.4bn; $1.6bn of 2019 sales, $221m pre-tax gain Originally planned as a spin-off or IPO; executed as a cash sale, with about $200m of exit and stranded cost
Q1 2020 Electrical Products and Electrical Systems and Services become Electrical Americas and Electrical Global; filtration, golf grips and aerospace connectors move into Aerospace; acquisition and divestiture charges move to Corporate $436m of FY2019 Aerospace revenue arrived by transfer. Segment margins before and after are on different bases
2 Aug 2021 Hydraulics sold to Danfoss at $3.3bn, 13.2x 2019 EBITDA; $3.1bn net of cash sold, about $450m of cash taxes The highest exit multiple of Eaton's disposals, and the funding for Tripp Lite and Cobham
Mar–Jun 2021 Tripp Lite $1,651m, Cobham Mission Systems $2,800m $4.5bn of acquisitions in one year, redeploying the divestiture proceeds
Q1 2023 "Megaproject" enters the earnings-call vocabulary — zero mentions Q4 2015 through Q4 2022, fifteen in Q1 2023 Electrical Americas margin expanded 400 basis points that year on 19% organic growth
1 Jun 2025 Paulo Ruiz becomes CEO; Gregory Page becomes non-executive Chairman The guidance record through 2024 was set by a different CEO and CFO
26 Jan 2026 Intention to separate Mobility announced Ten months after publishing 2030 margin targets of 20% for Vehicle and 16% for eMobility
23 Jan – 12 Mar 2026 Ultra PCS closed at $1,529m; Boyd Thermal closed at $9,549m $11,079m of acquisition cash in one quarter, funded with $8,500m of US notes, €1,200m of euro notes and commercial paper
6 Mar 2026 $8,500m of senior notes issued in six tranches, 3.85% 2028 to 5.45% 2056 The term stack's principal-weighted coupon moved from 3.51% to 4.13% in six months
10 Jun 2026 Definitive Reverse Morris Trust agreements with Dana; close expected Q1 2027 Structure changed from the plain spin-off announced in January. Eaton receives about $1.1bn of cash and its shareholders take at least 50.1% of the combined company

Five inflections.

  • Cooper Industries, November 2012. The decision was Eaton's own, and two consequences persist: Eaton became an electrical company, and the Irish domicile created both the tax position analysts probed in 2016 and the 25% Irish dividend withholding exposure.
  • The portfolio subtraction of 2016–2021. Revenue went from $19,747m to $27,448m and total segment operating profit from $2,958m to $6,713m, with segment margin from 15.0% to 24.5% and cyclical mobile businesses from 27.2% of sales to 11.3%. Return on capital, measured as NOPAT over total assets less current liabilities, rose from 8.3% to 13.8%.
  • COVID and the 2020 re-segmentation. Revenue declined from $21,390m to $17,858m; on the restated basis segment operating profit went from $3,711m to $2,937m, a 21.9% decremental against a 25–30% guided range. Eaton withdrew guidance, cut executive base salaries 25–50% and the board cash retainer 50% for Q2, froze hiring, cut capital expenditure from a $550m plan to $389m, and took $214m of restructuring charges. The dividend was maintained and had already been raised 3% in February. Eaton has not reduced the declared dividend in the twelve years of record.
  • The data-centre step-change, 2023. Electrical Americas margin expanded 400 basis points in one year on 19% organic growth, attributed in the FY2023 10-K to higher sales volumes and net price realisation. Company segment margin went 20.2%, 22.0%, 24.0%, 24.5%.
  • The portfolio remade and the balance sheet levered, January–June 2026. Total assets went from $41,251m to $56,181m, goodwill from $15,769m to $20,229m, other intangibles from $5,054m to $12,611m, total debt from $9,895m to $20,611m. Net interest expense was $201m in Q2 2026 against $71m a year earlier and intangible amortisation $255m against $129m; total corporate expense rose 68% in both Q2 and H1. Net income attributable to shareholders declined 13% in H1 on 19% more revenue.

How Eaton has behaved. Downturns are met with cost, and the dividend and the portfolio are left alone: 2015–16 and 2020 show the same sequence of front-loaded restructuring, cut discretionary and capital spending, and a maintained and raised dividend. Portfolio subtraction is denied until it happens — the April 2016 statement on a break-up, the April 2017 and February 2020 statements that Vehicle is core, and the March 2025 publication of 2030 Vehicle and eMobility margin targets each preceded an exit. Windfalls go into acquisitions: the $600m from Cummins, the $1.4bn from Signify and the $3.1bn from Danfoss were each followed within eighteen months by a purchase of similar or larger size. Investor-day targets have been set low and beaten, then not refreshed: against the March 2020 five-year plan the CFO's own grading in March 2025 was "in revenue, we did about 4x what we had planned; in terms of EPS CAGR, about twice."

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

10.1 Who runs Eaton

Four of the five current named executive officers took their seat within about two years. Paulo Ruiz became CEO on 1 June 2025 after joining Eaton in April 2019 as Hydraulics Group President, running Energy Solutions and Services from 2021, the Industrial Sector from 2022 and the company as President and COO from September 2024; Craig Arnold retired at the mandatory officer retirement age of 65 after nine years as CEO. David Foster became CFO on 2 March 2026, a 29-year Eaton veteran returning from outside. Gregory Page, a director since 2003 and Lead Director from 2022, became non-executive Chairman when the roles were split on Arnold's retirement.

The CFO seat has turned over four times in six years against one CEO change. Olivier Leonetti was hired in February 2024 with a $271,667 cash bonus and $9.6m of make-whole equity, reported $11.8m of 2024 and $5.1m of 2025 compensation, and ceased to be CFO twenty-five months later. Ruiz described the change as "part of a planned transition" on the Q4 2025 call and, five months later, said "I did recognize it in my own team, my executive team, we needed to set the tone from the top and lead by example. So we looked and strengthened my executive team for faster results."

10.2 What the plan measures

The annual cash incentive pays on adjusted EPS and adjusted operating cash flow, plus a business-unit and individual factor, in a range of 0–300% of target. FY2025 targets were adjusted EPS of $12.00 and adjusted operating cash flow of $4,800m against actuals of $12.07 and $4,472m. The long-term incentive is 50% performance share units earned entirely on relative total shareholder return against a sixteen-company peer group, plus 25% restricted stock units and 25% options vesting on service. Share-ownership requirements are 6x salary for the CEO and 4x for the CFO and Electrical COO; hedging and pledging are prohibited outright; clawback covers restatements and misconduct.

Neither plan measures return on capital, organic growth, margin or backlog conversion. That is the result of two dated decisions: in 2016 the long-term performance criteria changed from adjusted EPS growth and Cash Flow Return on Gross Capital, equally weighted, to 100% relative total shareholder return, with the first award period beginning 1 January 2016; and in February 2021 the short-term metric Cash Flow Return on Gross Capital, in use since 1993 and described by Eaton as "an internal measure of return on capital", was replaced by adjusted operating cash flow because "it is a complex, proprietary measure that contains competitive information and is not disclosed publicly."

The acquisition test is written in the same currency. Adjusted EPS excludes intangible amortisation, so the $7,190m of intangibles Boyd created does not touch the accretion test or the bonus metric; interest expense does flow through, so leverage is not free.

The formula is advisory. The Committee overrode it in six of the last seven years — 96% to 90% (2019), 0% to 50% (2020), 177% to 125% (2021), 58% to 83% (2022), 136% to 123% (2024), 96% to 70% (2025) — four of them downward. The FY2025 cut removed a gain arising from the Fibrebond acquisition, real-estate transactions and deferred cash payments. Long-term awards have paid above target in seven consecutive completed periods, from 130% to 189%, averaging about 166%; the 2023–2025 period paid 138% on Eaton's 113.55% total shareholder return, sixth of seventeen companies.

Insider ownership is small. All directors and executive officers together beneficially owned 394,737 shares at 1 February 2026, which the proxy states is 0.10% of the class, about $178m at the 14 August 2026 price. Across ninety-two Form 4 filings covering February 2025 to August 2026, open-market sales were 253,676 shares for $86.4m and open-market purchases were 1,561 shares for $0.6m, all seven purchases by one non-employee director. Arnold sold $49.0m three weeks before retiring at $305–324 and Ruiz sold $4.2m at about $390, both against $451.51 on 14 August 2026, and most sales were funded by option exercises at strikes of $98–171. Say-on-pay support has run 92–94% for seven years.

10.3 Candor

Management quantifies its own misses and volunteers items that flatter a beat. On the Q2 2026 call Ruiz interrupted the Q&A to address tariff refunds before being asked — "our impact in Q2 from the IEEPA refunds is less than $3 million... it's a clearly operational beat" — and corrected the transcript figure to "$2.8 million, if you want to be precise." On Q3 2025 he sized an Electrical Americas revenue shortfall as "$80 million, 8-0." On Q1 2026 he disclosed the guidance cut with the number attached: "our guidance range of 24.1% to 24.5% is 50 basis points lower than the prior guide." And he named the predecessor's growth record directly: "it took us 100-plus years, 112 years to hit $20 billion in top line when we acquired Cooper. Then the following decade, you guys know as well, we didn't grow much."

Where the account has changed is content per megawatt (§6.4) and the framing of AI dependence. At the March 2025 investor day the CFO said "If we look at our order backlog today, 20% is based upon AI, meaning 80% is not based upon AI... the Electrical Americas growth in the data center, which we expect to see growing at about 15%, is not going to depend on AI." Eleven months later, on the Q4 2025 call: "we already saw the orders in 2025 were 50-50. So 50% of our orders were cloud-based data center growth. The other half were AI." Management reported the change plainly; the framing behind the 2030 plan no longer describes the order book. Confidence language per thousand words on the earnings call is running roughly four and a half times the 2024 rate, and the escalation begins on the Q3 2025 call, the first of the two quarters in which organic growth landed below its guided range.

Ten-year free cash flow was $25,193m. Against it, dividends absorbed 50%, buybacks 41%, gross acquisitions 32% and acquisitions net of divestiture proceeds 14%. Two divestitures funded most of the decade's acquisitions.

The buyback responded to cash on hand. Across 2016–2020 Eaton spent $5,488m to retire 70.4m shares at an average $77.96; across 2021–2023, $408m for 2.9m shares at $140.69; across 2024–2025, $4,354m for 13.5m shares at $322.52. The 2024–2025 pair spent 42% of the decade's buyback dollars to retire 16% of the decade's shares, at roughly 31–34x trailing GAAP earnings against about 15x in 2016–2019. Buyback dollars tracked operating cash flow, which was $2,163m in 2021 and $2,533m in 2022 — the Tripp Lite and Cobham years — and $3,624m, $4,327m and $4,472m in 2023–2025. FY2023 tests that directly: no acquisitions, no repurchases, and cash plus short-term investments rising $2,054m to $2,609m, against the framework the CFO stated a year later — "We do not want cash to build in our balance sheet." Measured by outcome the programme has made money: 86.8m shares retired for $10,250m would be worth $39,192m at the 14 August 2026 price.

Capital intensity rose from 2.5% of revenue in 2016 to 3.3% in 2025 and about 3.5% guided for 2026, with capex at 1.93x property, plant and equipment depreciation in FY2025, so growth capex was roughly $440m of the $919m spent [estimate: PP&E depreciation as the maintenance proxy]. The CFO said at the 2025 investor day that capital intensity peaks in 2026 and returns to "our historical CapEx rate, about 2.5% of revenue" in the back half of the plan; the Q2 2026 10-Q states Eaton "plans to increase capital expenditures over the next several years to expand production capacity."

Per-share outcomes over FY2016–FY2025: revenue grew 3.7% a year and revenue per diluted share 5.5%; GAAP diluted EPS 10.7%; free cash flow 6.2% and free cash flow per share 8.0%; the declared dividend 6.9%; and diluted shares declined 1.7% a year. Share-count reduction added about 1.8 points a year to every per-share line, roughly 17% of the EPS growth rate. That contribution stops in 2026: repurchases are guided to nil, the share count is guided flat, and GAAP EPS is guided to $10.36–$10.56 against $10.45 in FY2025.

Dividend increases declared: 4% (2021), 7%, 6%, 9%, 11%, 6% (2026). The 2026 raise is the smallest since 2023 against adjusted EPS growth guided at about 12%, so the payout ratio steps down again in the year Eaton levered up. Cash payout was 54% of net income in FY2016 and 40% in FY2025, 34% of adjusted earnings, inside the 30–50% band the CFO set in March 2025.

Free cash flow conversion is the commitment furthest from its target and the one that has been missed. FY2025 free cash flow of $3,553m against adjusted earnings of $4,722m is 75%, and the FY2026 guide of $3.9–4.3bn against roughly $5,250m implies about 78%, against a 95–100% commitment for 2030.▪ FY2025 free cash flow landed below the guided $3.7–4.1bn range. Inventory has moved the other way, from $4,227m at end-2024 to $5,417m at 30 June 2026, and extending payables runs into the supply-chain finance programme already inside accounts payable.

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

Eaton was a disciplined serial acquirer through 2022 and has been running a different programme since March 2025. Both halves are supported by figures Eaton published.

On the disciplined side, no goodwill impairment charge appears in any 10-K from FY2016 through FY2025; every annual test concluded that reporting-unit fair values "substantially exceed their respective carrying amounts." The one clear disappointment is small: Green Motion, bought in March 2021 for $106m including $57m of contingent consideration, where the earn-out was written down to $6m by 31 December 2024 as revenue milestones were missed, an effective price near $55m. Entry multiples on every deal of scale between 2019 and 2025 were in a narrow band of roughly 12x to 14x EBITDA, and the two exits bracketed it — Hydraulics above at 13.2x 2019 EBITDA, Lighting below at roughly 7.5x trailing on an analyst's figure. Cooper delivered $393m of annual synergies against a $375m original underwriting, after a raise to $475m and a cut back to $393m for slower end markets.

On the changed side, Eaton paid $11,079m of cash for acquisitions in the first six months of 2026, more than the $8,029m spent across the seven years 2019 through 2025 combined. Boyd Thermal was bought at 22.5x its estimated 2026 adjusted EBITDA, roughly 60% above the top of that band, and is expected to be accretive to adjusted earnings only in year two.▪ The published hurdle moved from a minimum of 300 basis points over an 8–9% cost of capital to 200–300 basis points, and the accretion window from one year to two, while the CFO described the filter as unchanged. Goodwill and other intangibles reached $32,840m at 30 June 2026 against $20,254m of Eaton shareholders' equity, so tangible book value is negative by roughly $12.6bn.

The 2026 programme has no outcomes yet. Eaton lowered its published hurdle and lengthened its published accretion window while describing the filter as the same.

Synergies. Eaton published a dollar synergy target and reported against it once, on Cooper. For every deal since it has published an entry multiple and an accretion year instead. Boyd, the largest cash acquisition Eaton has ever made, was announced with a 22.5x multiple and year-two accretion, and no bridge from 22.5x to the "high single digit" post-synergy figure has been published. The one third-party synergy commitment among these deals belongs to the counterparty: Dana committed to $250m of run-rate savings within twenty-four months, and its CEO said "it doesn't say approximately anywhere, it just says $250 million."

Purchase-price allocations are provisional for longer than the headline multiple suggests. Cobham's preliminary intangibles of $1,575m were cut to $1,462m and goodwill raised from $1,088m to $1,264m; Tripp Lite's intangibles went $630m to $604m; Royal Power's $306m to $341m; Fibrebond's goodwill $572m to $540m; and Boyd's intangibles were raised $1,603m from $5,587m to $7,190m with goodwill cut by the same amount inside a single quarter, and the 10-Q states the allocation is preliminary and revisions "could have a material impact." The Boyd allocation also brought $1,866m of other noncurrent liabilities.

Post-deal performance. Fibrebond has performed best: underwritten on $110m of 2025 estimated adjusted EBITDA and delivering $156m of segment operating profit in nine months, which annualises near $208m and puts the effective entry multiple closer to 7x than the 12.7x published. Ultra PCS delivered a 27.9% margin against the segment's 22.8% in Q2 2026. Boyd delivered 23.1% against the 25% adjusted EBITDA margin underwritten, and Electrical Global's reported margin still declined from 20.1% to 19.8% in Q2 because the legacy base declined about 100 basis points while Boyd added roughly 70 [estimate: backing Boyd's Q2 sales and profit out of the segment at the period margin]. Souriau reported $287m of sales in 2020 against the $363m trailing base at signing, because the aerospace market collapsed three months after closing. Tripp Lite, Cobham and Souriau have not been disclosed separately since their first partial year.

Exits against entries. Hydraulics went at 13.2x 2019 EBITDA, above every entry multiple Eaton paid between 2019 and 2025. Lighting was acquired inside Cooper at a blended 2.4x sales and 11–12x EBITDA and sold at 0.9x sales; Arnold's answer to that comparison was that the disaggregated Lighting price "is not an awful lot different than what we sold it for", and Eaton has not published the disaggregated figure. Mobility is being exchanged: measured against Eaton's own reported FY2025 segment EBITDA of $528m the $5,100m enterprise value is 9.7x, and 6.6x fully synergised, against Dana's stated 8.3x and 5.9x on a $614m 2026 estimate. The gap between the two EBITDA bases is $86–106m, or 2.6 to 3.2 points of margin, and neither party reconciled it on the call.

Two structures changed after announcement: Lighting from a planned spin-off or IPO to a cash sale, and Mobility from the spin-off announced on 26 January 2026 to the Reverse Morris Trust signed on 10 June 2026, with a plain spin-off as the stated fallback. No deal Eaton announced in this period was terminated and no regulator-forced remedy appears in the filings.

Every instrument is senior unsecured. There are no convertibles, no secured notes, no preferred shares outstanding and no floating-rate term debt. The 2026 issues are stated at face and the December 2025 instruments at their carrying value then, so euro carrying values at 30 June 2026 differ on translation. The 0.128% euro notes due 2026, $1,057m at year-end, were repaid inside the $1,143m of payments on borrowings in H1 2026.

Weighted-average cost of debt. The principal-weighted coupon on the term stack is 4.13%: $8,841m of surviving legacy notes at 3.91% and $9,890m of March 2026 issues at 4.33%, against 3.51% for the whole stack at 31 December 2025. Adding $2,088m of commercial paper at an assumed 3.5–4.5% gives an all-in rate of 4.07–4.17%. Everything is fixed-coupon and paid semi-annually on the dollar notes and annually on the euro notes, so cash and accrual interest do not differ; interest paid on debt was $351m in 2025, $329m in 2024 and $319m in 2023. That computed rate reconciles to the reported line: $18.5bn at 4.13% is $764m, plus $84m on commercial paper, less perhaps $30m of interest income, against a Q2 2026 net interest expense of $201m and an $804m annual run-rate.

Refinancing and the maturity wall. Nothing material matures before the $700m of 3.10% notes in 2027, and the heaviest year is 2036 at about $2,587m. The March 2026 issuance priced the full curve at 3.85% at two years to 5.45% at thirty, and the surviving legacy book averages 3.91%, so refinancing the whole term stack at that curve would cost roughly 20 basis points more, about $37m a year pre-tax. The market's own view is close: fair value of long-term debt including the current portion was $18,013m against $18,520m carrying at 30 June 2026, a 2.7% discount. Eaton disclosed that a 100 basis point rise in rates would have cut the market value of its debt by $617m on a $9,894m book at 31 December 2025, an implied duration of about 6.2 years.

Security, guarantees and covenants. The 10-Q states that Eaton has no material long-term secured debt and that substantially all of the senior notes, which comprise substantially all of Eaton's long-term indebtedness, together with the credit facilities are guaranteed by Eaton and 17 of its subsidiaries on a joint and several basis. Those guarantees are effectively subordinated to any future secured debt and structurally subordinated to the liabilities of non-guarantor subsidiaries, and they release automatically in defined circumstances. The 2012 and 2017 Indentures require any subsidiary that becomes a borrower or guarantor under any debt series or syndicated facility to become a guarantor; the 2022 and 2025 Indentures set that trigger at a subsidiary guaranteeing or issuing indebtedness of less than 25% of Eaton's total outstanding indebtedness, a weaker accretion mechanism. Exhibit 22 lists the guarantors and is referenced without being reproduced.

There is no financial maintenance covenant on leverage, coverage or net worth. The binding term is a negative pledge: at Eaton's present credit rating level the most restrictive financial covenant limits secured debt to 10% of adjusted consolidated net worth, and secured debt is nil. The constraint on the balance sheet is the rating agencies and management's preference; nothing accelerates if leverage rises. The clause is conditioned on the current rating level, and Eaton does not state where that threshold sits.

Trailing EBITDA includes only 110 days of Boyd and 158 of Ultra PCS; annualising both adds roughly $320m and puts pro-forma leverage at about 2.9x [estimate: Boyd $121m over 110/365 plus Ultra PCS $31m over 158/365, less the amounts already in the trailing figure]. Either figure is above the 1.26–2.57x band of the prior ten years, which averaged 1.85x. The 2020 reading of 2.57x is the closest historical comparison and it came from collapsing EBITDA on a 16.5% revenue decline; total debt declined that year. This one comes entirely from borrowing.

Ratings held A-/A-2 at S&P for the whole decade, with the outlook negative through 2017 and stable since; Moody's upgraded from Baa1 to A3 in 2023 at the bottom of the leverage cycle. Both were stable as of the FY2025 10-K, filed 26 February 2026 — after the Boyd financing was arranged and two weeks before it closed. No post-close agency action appears in any archived filing, and neither 2026 10-Q repeats the ratings table.

Liquidity. Cash $483m and short-term investments $212m at 30 June 2026, against a $4,000m revolving credit facility expiring 27 September 2030, undrawn, upsized from $3,000m on 6 February 2026, plus $872m of uncommitted lines. Commercial paper of $2,088m is the first material position since 2016 and part-funds a permanent asset; treating the revolver as reserved against it, unencumbered liquidity is roughly $2.6bn. Cash plus short-term investments is 3.4% of total debt, the thinnest of the decade against 28.1% in 2023. An $8,000m delayed-draw term loan signed on 6 February 2026 was terminated undrawn on 6 March once the bonds priced, with no fees or penalties.

Leases and pension. Operating lease liabilities were $870m at 30 June 2026 with an 8.0-year weighted-average term at a 4.7% discount rate, and finance leases of $25m are included in long-term debt. Sale-leasebacks of non-production facilities produced gains of $38m (2025), $56m (2024) and $53m (2023), booked in other income. One off-balance-sheet item: a March 2025 non-cancellable synthetic lease on a manufacturing facility with construction costs of approximately $185m, on which Eaton is construction agent, commencing on completion expected in H1 2027, with a residual value guarantee of approximately 85% of construction cost, roughly $157m. Retirement plans were underfunded by $671m at 31 December 2025 against $748m a year earlier, 86.3% funded in aggregate, with contributions of $124m in 2025 and $9m of expected US contributions in 2026. Two assumption changes flatter reported income without affecting cash: the expected long-term return on US plan assets went from 6.50% for 2024 to 7.00% for 2025 to 7.50% for 2026. US non-union plans are frozen to further accrual for cash-balance participants from 1 January 2021 and final-average-pay participants from 1 January 2026.

Share count. Equity compensation is small and the count is set by buyback policy. Pre-tax share-based compensation was $126m in FY2025, 0.46% of revenue and 3.1% of net income, against $108m and $97m in the two prior years. Gross issuance under equity plans was 0.18% of shares in 2025, 0.33% in 2024 and 0.38% in 2023, so offsetting dilution costs about $230m a year at 2025 prices, 12% of the FY2025 buyback. Period-end shares went 449.4m (2016), 398.1m (2020), 399.4m (2023), 387.9m (2025) and 388.4m at 30 June 2026 — a 13.7% decline over the decade delivered in two bursts separated by a three-year pause. Eaton states it does not intend to repurchase shares in 2026 because of Boyd; $7,597m remained available under the $9.0bn 2025 programme at 31 December 2025. The Mobility split-off works the other way, retiring Eaton shares tendered in exchange for SpinCo shares: at 8–10x Mobility EBITDA less the $1.1bn of debt, at $451.51 and a 7–8% exchange discount, that is roughly 9m to 12m shares, 2.3–3.1% of the count [estimate: Mobility 2026E EBITDA of $627m from Dana's disclosed revenue and margin; every input is an assumption and the bounds are quoted with it]. A separate derivation from the disclosed $4.0bn equity component at $451.51 with no discount gives up to about 8.9m shares. There are no convertible instruments and no preferred shares outstanding.

Structural risks, ranked by size of the exposure.

  1. Interest expense re-rates the earnings bridge. Net interest went from $71m in Q2 2025 to $201m in Q2 2026 and from $103m to $307m for the half, against $241m for the whole of FY2025. At the Q2 run-rate the annual figure is about $804m, roughly $2.07 a share pre-tax on 388.4m shares, and all of it is booked at Corporate below segment operating profit.
  2. Rating pressure without a covenant trigger. Leverage of 2.9–3.1x is well above the band that supported the 2023 upgrade. No debt accelerates if the rating declines; the 10% secured-debt covenant is expressly conditioned on the present rating level.
  3. Commercial paper funding a permanent asset. $2,088m of a $4,000m programme against $695m of cash and short-term investments, backstopped 1.9x by the undrawn revolver. The exposure is that the cheapest tranche of the acquisition funding reprices every 30 to 90 days.
  4. Tax contingencies exceed the reserve on the disclosed notices. Gross unrecognised income tax benefits were $1,300m at 31 December 2025 plus $218m of accrued interest and penalties. The IRS 2011–2013 Statutory Notice alone proposes $749m of additional taxes plus $110m of penalties, and Eaton says the same issues recur in the 2014–2016 exam and the open 2017–2019 exam, where the total potential impact "is not estimable." Two Brazilian goodwill-amortisation cases add $22m plus $62m and $24m plus $82m, against which Eaton has pledged $17m of real estate, $101m of bonds and a $28m cash deposit.
  5. Floating-rate exposure, small and now a cost. All term debt is fixed and the $2,088m of commercial paper is 10.1% of total debt, so 100 basis points is about $21m pre-tax. At 31 December 2025 a 100 basis point rise in short rates would have decreased net pre-tax interest expense by $8m because floating-rate investments exceeded floating-rate debt; with $2,088m of paper against $695m of cash and investments it now costs roughly $14m [estimate: ($2,088m − $695m) × 1%].
  6. Structural subordination. Seventeen subsidiaries guarantee, the newer indentures use a weaker accretion trigger, and Eaton does not disclose what share of consolidated assets or liabilities is outside the guarantor group.
  7. Commodity exposure is close to unhedged. A hypothetical 10% commodity move produces under $1m of gain or loss on Eaton's own disclosure, against 470 basis points of Electrical Americas margin lost to commodity inflation in H1 2026. Eaton manages copper through price.
  8. Supply-chain finance inside payables. Obligations went $398m (1 Jan 2025) to $543m (1 Jan 2026) to $669m (30 Jun 2026), 12% of the $5,421m payables balance. The $145m increase in 2025 flattered operating cash flow by that amount, 3% of the reported $4,472m.
  9. Synthetic lease residual guarantee. Roughly $157m, with nothing on the balance sheet until the lease commences in H1 2027.

13.4 What drove the decade

Revenue grew 3.7% a year across FY2016–FY2025 and 9.0% a year across FY2020–FY2025, and neither rate describes the underlying business on its own: FY2020 revenue of $17,858m was below FY2016's $19,747m because Lighting and Automotive Fluid Conveyance were sold while COVID cut organic sales 11%, and the Lighting and Hydraulics exits took 7, 10 and 7 points out of reported growth in FY2020, FY2021 and FY2022. Diluted EPS grew 10.7% a year and adjusted EPS 19.7% a year from the FY2020 base.

Gross margin widened 540 basis points over the decade, from 32.2% to 37.6%, and computed operating margin 740 basis points, from 11.6% to 19.0%; the extra 200 basis points is operating leverage on selling, administrative and research expense, which took 20.5% of revenue in FY2016 and 18.6% in FY2025. Net margin widened only 520 basis points because the effective tax rate rose from 9.4% to 17.1%. Eaton's own gross-margin attribution: FY2023 +320 basis points on higher sales volumes and net price realisation; FY2024 +180 on +290 from higher sales, +90 from operating efficiencies, −100 from commodity and wage inflation and −70 from growth-initiative costs; FY2025 −60 on +260 from higher sales, −280 from commodity and wage inflation and −50 from acquisition and divestiture charges.

Working capital days moved in opposite directions and cancelled: inventory days rose from 62 to 95 and payable days from 47 to 84, so the cash conversion cycle is unchanged at 78 days, with the caveat that the supply-chain finance programme inside payables makes the 84-day figure partly a financing arrangement. Free cash flow over net income averaged 1.18x across FY2016–FY2020 and 0.84x across FY2021–FY2025; most of the decline is the working-capital cost of growth, with FY2025 operating cash flow absorbing $420m of receivable growth, $256m of inventory growth and $357m of unbilled receivables against $332m from payables.

Return on invested capital moved from 9.3% (FY2016) to 15.9% (FY2025) on this section's definition, while return on capital excluding goodwill and intangibles ran between 44% and 72% on that same narrower invested-capital base. The gap between the two is the price paid for acquired revenue, and it widened again in H1 2026 as goodwill and other intangibles rose $12.0bn against $11.1bn of cash paid.

Six features of the reported history:

  • Return on capital is 15.9% against the 21.6% return on equity more often quoted, and FY2017's 13.8% includes a $1,077m disposal gain that takes it to 9.7% when removed.
  • Margin expansion stopped in FY2025 and reversed in H1 2026. Gross margin peaked at 38.2% in FY2024, Electrical Americas at 30.2%, and Electrical's incremental margin declined from 50% in FY2024 to 29% in FY2025 and 12% in H1 2026 excluding Boyd.
  • The adjusted-to-GAAP gap doubled in one year, from $1.62 in FY2025 to a guided $3.04 in FY2026, and the largest add-back is the amortisation created by $11.1bn of cash spending.
  • Backlog is growing partly because it is lengthening. Total backlog went from about $13bn to about $19.8bn between December 2023 and December 2025 while the share targeted for delivery within twelve months declined from 76% to 69%, and 71% at 30 June 2026.
  • Balance-sheet capacity was consumed in six months. Total debt went from $9,895m to $20,611m and net debt to EBITDA from 1.47x to 3.09x.
  • FY2025's 8% organic growth is two quarters out of date as a starting point. Q1 2026 was 10% organic and Q2 was 14%, with full-year guidance raised twice to 11–13%.

Order intake turned two quarters before revenue did and four before margin: Electrical Americas trailing organic orders went from −4% in Q1 2025 to 42% in Q1 2026 while segment margin went from 30.0% to 25.6%, because the capacity ramp and the commodity increase both landed before the volume converted. Across 23 analysts the CY2026 EPS range spans 3.3% of the mean, while 27 price targets span 42.6% of their mean.

Management against its own record. Across eighteen quarters of numeric organic guidance Eaton landed above the midpoint thirteen times and below the range twice, both in the second half of 2025.▪ Across seventeen quarters of segment-margin guidance it landed above the midpoint fifteen times and below the range never; across twenty-two quarters of adjusted EPS, above nineteen times and below never. The beat has compressed: adjusted-EPS outperformance against the guided midpoint averaged 4.5% across Q1 2021–Q4 2022, 5.9% across Q1 2023–Q2 2024 and 1.5% across the last eight quarters, and segment-margin outperformance from 69 to 33 basis points over the same spans. Full-year adjusted EPS beat the original guide by 10.7% in 2023, 6.4% in 2024 and 0.6% in 2025. FY2025 free cash flow of $3.6bn landed below the guided $3.7–4.1bn, the only full-year range miss in the six-year record.

Where the FY2026 guidance is stretched. Electrical Americas needs an H2 margin near 31.2% against 26.6% in H1, a step of about 460 basis points of which 300 is price sticking against copper, with all pricing actions implemented in Q2 or early August. The implied Q4 organic growth at the full-year midpoint is roughly 9% against a Q3 guide of 13.5–15.5%, a five-point deceleration of which about two points is the comparison base. And Mobility needs roughly +9% to +13% organic in H2 against about −4% in H1 [estimate: H1 2025 Mobility of about $1,623m and H2 2025 of about $1,486m, backed out from the disclosed organic and currency contributions].

Where the street's number does not describe the company that will report it. Consensus CY2027 revenue of $36,154m keeps roughly $3.2bn of Mobility in a year the Reverse Morris Trust is expected to close in the first quarter. Removing three of four quarters, about $2.4bn [estimate: $2.1–3.1bn depending on close timing; three-quarters of the H1 2026 annualised run-rate as the midpoint], leaves CY2027 at roughly $33.8bn and growth of about 4%. The same gap does not appear in EPS: Mobility earned $198m on $1,607m in H1 2026, so removing it lifts the implied CY2027 operating margin about 60 basis points, and netting the forgone profit against interest saved on $1.1bn and the share retirement leaves CY2027 adjusted EPS near $15.70 against the printed $15.82 [estimate: consensus adjusted net income less three quarters of Mobility profit taxed at 24%, plus interest saved, over a share count reduced by up to 8.9m].

The 2030 plan and the portfolio it was struck for. The March 2025 targets assumed five segments and no acquisition contribution. From the FY2025 base of $27,448m the $38bn revenue target is a 6.7% CAGR, inside the guided band; from an ex-Mobility base of $24,339m it is 9.3%, above the top of it. Either the target falls to roughly $34.5bn [estimate: $38bn less Mobility grown at 2–3% to 2030] or the Electrical and Aerospace ambition rose without being restated. Management reaffirmed the 2026 and 2030 commitments on 31 July 2026 and has said it is "too early to provide new targets for 2030", with no investor day planned for 2026.▪

What the analysts asked. Ten analysts asked questions on the 31 July 2026 call. Two questions dominated: whether the second-half margin bridge can be delivered on flat sequential revenue, which the CFO answered with a testable quarter-by-quarter walk landing Q3 at 30.0%; and whether the growth is broader than data centres, which Deane Dray opened and Chris Snyder quantified by naming his own miss — "Electrical Global organic growth, which was the biggest upside surprise in our model... high teens organic versus high singles expectations." The effective tax rate, which cost $0.15 of Q2 EPS against a $0.25 segment beat, came up in none of the ten questions.

The move began the session before the print: Eaton rose 6.9% on 30 July alongside GEV +9.1% and NVT +8.4%, so part of the two-session gain is a sector move [web]

Two reactions just inside the band show the same asymmetry: Q2 2024 beat its guidance midpoint by 6.2% and the stock declined 2.3% on the day and 8.0% over two sessions; Q3 2024 beat by 2.2% and declined 3.3%.

The multiple across three periods. Through 2016–2019 there was no re-rating: forward P/E on adjusted EPS held a 14.6x median in an 11.1x–19.3x range while sales were flat and the portfolio work was subtraction. Across 2020–2022 the forward multiple moved from a 10.9x COVID trough to the low 20s as the Hydraulics sale and the Tripp Lite and Cobham purchases changed the mix, with a +43.8% price return in FY2021 on 35% adjusted-EPS growth. Since January 2023 the forward P/E median is 25.9x against 14.6x in 2016–2019, in a 16.4x–31.6x range, standing at 30.3x on 14 August 2026, within 1.3 points of the decade high.

These forward multiples are based on consensus estimates, and consensus adjusted EPS matches the guidance midpoint, $13.49 against $13.50. Estimate dispersion widens sharply beyond the guided year: FY2026 runs $13.25 low, $13.51 mean, $13.70 high across 23 analysts, a 33.0x–34.1x band; FY2027 runs $15.00 low, $16.02 mean, $17.30 high across 22 analysts, a 26.1x–30.1x band four times as wide [web]. No consensus EBITDA series was obtainable, so no forward EV/EBITDA is stated; on trailing figures EV/EBITDA is roughly 30x [estimate: EV $195,282m over trailing EBITDA of about $6,500m, built as FY2025 less H1 2025 plus H1 2026; range $6,400–6,600m gives 29.6x–30.5x], and that denominator holds only three and a half months of Boyd.

Consensus revisions went in opposite directions by year. Over the twelve months to 14 August 2026 CY2026 adjusted EPS was cut 1.4% from $13.68 to $13.49, while CY2027 rose 4.3% and CY2028 rose 8.0% with the steps widening at every horizon. The near year came down as the street converged onto an initial guide that was below its prior number, then followed two raises. In the two weeks after the Q2 print the street added revenue and took out margin: CY2027 revenue rose $824m while operating profit declined $75m, taking the implied CY2027 margin down 70 basis points.

Fiscal-year-end price to book ranged from 1.9x (FY2018) to 7.2x (FY2024) with a 3.5x median and stood at 8.6x against 30 June 2026 book value at the 14 August price. Two accounting features limit what it says: goodwill and other intangibles were $20,823m of $41,251m of total assets at 31 December 2025 and grew again with Boyd and Ultra PCS, and Eaton has repurchased $7.4bn of stock since FY2019.

15.7 How Eaton trades

Daily-return correlation with Vertiv rose from 0.54 in 2022–2023 to 0.80 in 2024–2025 and 0.75 in 2026 to date, while correlation with Illinois Tool Works declined from 0.68 to 0.33 to 0.29 across the same windows. Beta to the S&P 500 rose from 0.96 to 1.50 to 1.73 and realised annualised volatility from 27.4% to 33.1% to 41.8%. The 2026 advance decomposes mostly to the multiple: forward P/E went from 23.2x at the 2025 year-end to 30.3x on 14 August 2026, a 1.30x move, while twelve-month-forward adjusted EPS went from $13.70 to $14.93, a 1.09x move. And every metric named in the two largest positive reaction days — data-centre revenue growth, order and backlog growth, the negotiation pipeline, the 307 GW US backlog, content per megawatt — is disclosed only in releases, calls and decks.

Eaton's enterprise value here uses Yahoo's total-debt field, which includes operating-lease liabilities, so it is $195,997m against the $195,282m built from the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet debt lines used in §15, a 0.4% difference.

17. Forward model summary

The model projects revenue by segment from explicit drivers through segment profit, corporate items, taxes, working capital, capital expenditure and free cash flow, with no multiple, no discounting and no per-share value. The base year is FY2025 and every FY2025 anchor ties to the filed figures in §13. Mobility is kept for one quarter of FY2027 and none thereafter, so two revenue lines are projected: total, and the surviving Electrical-plus-Aerospace company. No future acquisition is modelled, which makes the model silent on both the revenue Eaton says it will buy and the goodwill, amortisation and interest that buying it would add.

Aerospace is built from five channels on their own drivers, each growing at a different rate in the base: commercial OEM 7.0% a year on the certified Boeing and Airbus build rate; commercial aftermarket 7.5% on flight cycles against a commercial MRO market growing 6.6%; military OEM 6.2% on unit buys across five named platforms; military aftermarket and retrofit 7.8% against a $1bn 2025–2030 pipeline; and industrial filtration and golf grips 4.3% on industrial machinery utilisation. Weighted, that is 7.0–7.3% a year, matching Eaton's own 7% organic 2030 target and the aerospace-components reference-class median of 7.5%.

The model does not multiply gigawatts by $3.4m of content per megawatt. It sets a growth path for data-centre revenue and checks it against four external anchors: US private data-centre construction put in place at a $50.7bn annual rate in April 2026, up 46%; US data-centre power demand from about 31 GW in 2025 to 41 GW in 2026; US capacity commissioned of 8.5 GW in 2025 against 13.6 GW scheduled for 2026; and the 17% annual data-centre growth management says is inside its own 2030 plan. The base decays 38% in 2026 to 10% by 2030, a 21.0% compound rate from 2025, which is between the realised rate and the planning rate and converges on the planning rate by 2031.

Four of the five drivers that move the answer are Electrical, and the fifth is the tax rate. Aerospace at 15% of FY2025 revenue moves FY2032 segment profit by at most $152m, less than a third of what the data-centre driver moves. Two asymmetries: the data-centre sensitivity is skewed to the upside by $278m of segment profit because it compounds off a base that reaches 47% of Electrical Americas revenue by 2032; and working capital, which the CFO names as the largest of the three free-cash-flow levers, moves FY2032 free cash flow by only $52m for a 200 basis point change in intensity, because in a steady state the growth rate of revenue matters far more than the level of working capital. Working capital helps free cash flow while revenue growth decelerates and stops helping once growth stabilises.

17.5 Assumptions and where each is contested

Seventeen of these assumptions take the favourable side of the evidence, and the counter-argument for each is in the last column beside the number. The data-centre growth path, the Electrical Global growth and margin paths, the Boyd revenue path, the Electrical Americas 2026 and 2030 margins, the Aerospace commercial OEM and aftermarket rates, the Mobility 2026 rate, the corporate-expense roll-off, the amortisation decay, the adjusted tax rate, the capex glide, the working-capital ratio, the share count, the buyback and the leverage floor each face a live objection. Where the objection bears on a scenario bound, that is stated too.

The 2030 level puts Electrical Americas data centres alone at $10.0bn against a $7–10bn a year band implied by the pipeline at a 10–15% capture. The base is the highest of the five Aerospace channels and above the segment's own 7% target

The bear of −2% is the straight trend extrapolation and the better-supported base

The line absorbs all acquisition, divestiture and restructuring charges, and Eaton spent $12,596m in eighteen months while holding out roughly $21bn of capacity. The FY2026 guide itself moved from about $1,130m to $1,450m in a single quarter after two deals closed. The base also cuts corporate intensity from 4.4% of revenue in 2026 to 3.1% in 2030

Amortisation already went from $486m in FY2025 to $395m in H1 2026 alone

The bear of 4.7% absorbs roughly a one-notch downgrade

The bear of 25.0% reaches the realised H1 level
Tax rate on adjusted earnings 21.5% Structurally below the GAAP rate because Boyd's goodwill is not tax-deductible while the adjusted measure adds back amortisation pre-tax Every revision to date widened the gap: the FY2026 guide moved from 17.5–18.5% to 18.5–19.5% in one quarter and the realised H1 adjusted rate of about 23.8% still ran 430bp above the raised guide. The base splits the difference on a one-way series
Capital expenditure, FY2030 2.8% of revenue 70bp above the CFO's stated destination of about 2.5%, and the 95–100% free-cash-flow commitment requires capex to normalise The Q2 2026 10-Q states Eaton "plans to increase capital expenditures over the next several years to expand production capacity". The 2.5% historical reference matches 2016–2018 and not the 3.2–3.3% of 2023–2025, and six of the 24 capacity projects run beyond 2027. The bear of 3.2% is below the FY2026 guided level
Property, plant and equipment depreciation 2.0% of revenue The right point in the convergence: capex has run about 1.9x PP&E depreciation historically and the base's 2.8% capex against 2.0% depreciation already implies 1.4x The range is only 20bp wide on a moving base — FY2025 depreciation was 1.74% of revenue and the capacity programme is only partly in service. The line is absent from the sensitivity table, so the narrow span cannot change a conclusion
Net operating working capital, FY2030 21.8% of revenue Offsets are in use: deferred revenue nearly doubled to $1,159m, customer deposits rose 50% in FY2025, and the supply-chain finance programme is a live payables lever Every disclosed component moved the wrong way: FY2025 was 21.6% and 30 June 2026 was 22.2% of trailing revenue, days sales outstanding went 60 to 69, inventory rose 28% against 21% revenue growth, and unbilled receivables tripled. Systems mix mechanically builds unbilled receivables. The bear of 23.3% is only 110bp above the June 2026 actual
Diluted share count, FY2030 370.5m The ten-year record is −1.7% a year on $10,250m of buybacks against −1.06% a year on $10,600m over 2027–2032, correctly reflecting the same dollars buying fewer shares The 10.5m split-off retirement is above the 8.9m ceiling implied by the disclosed $4.0bn equity component at $451.51 with no discount, and it happens only if the exchange offer is subscribed. The 2027 buyback resumption depends on whether the tax-matters agreement restricts Eaton; Dana disclosed a 24-month prohibition on itself and no Eaton filing addresses the equivalent
Share repurchases, FY2030 $2,000m a year $2.0bn against $6,554m of 2030 base free cash flow is 31%, below the 41% ten-year average share and below the $2,492m spent in 2024 The series is bimodal and the base is smooth: three of the last six full years landed below $300m, every one an acquisition or cash-preservation year, so the bear of $900m is above all three observed floors. Revealed behaviour puts acquisitions first — $12,596m closed in eighteen months with buybacks at zero
Dividend per share +7.7%/yr FY2025–FY2032 Declared raises ran 4%, 7%, 6%, 9%, 11% and 6% from 2021 to 2026, and cash payout went from 54% of net income in FY2016 to 40% in FY2025 Compounding 8% after 2026 against base adjusted EPS compounding about 10% takes the payout to roughly 29.6% by FY2032, below the 30–50% band the CFO set. The band has never been binding on the low side
Net debt to EBITDA floor 1.5x from FY2030, identical in all three scenarios All three of the last pre-2026 years were at or below 1.5x and both agencies were stable at A−/A3 as of the FY2025 10-K The floor is below where Eaton has operated: the ten-year average is 1.85x and 1.5x was reached only in 2023, 2024 and 2025, when acquisition spending ran $0m, $50m and $1,490m against $11,079m in the first half of 2026. It also determines the answer it is meant to test, setting $14,633m of unallocated surplus, and with bear equal to base equal to bull the model cannot show what a company running 2.0–2.5x would do with the difference

The CY2027 and CY2028 revenue gaps are mostly definitional, because consensus keeps roughly $3.2bn of Mobility in CY2027 despite a Q1 2027 expected close. Adjusting for that, the base is roughly 2–3% below consensus revenue and 10–13% below on earnings.

Two of Eaton's own FY2026 guided lines do not reconcile with each other or with the reported history. The GAAP EPS guide midpoint of $10.46 needs a 16.3% full-year GAAP tax rate against 24.9% realised in H1, which implies an 8.8% H2 rate; closing the gap through profit instead needs a 25.4% full-year segment margin, a point above the top of the 24.1–24.5% guide. And the free-cash-flow guide of $3.9–4.3bn requires the change in net operating working capital to be about $412m on $5,231m of revenue growth, against $772m consumed on $2,570m of growth in FY2025; the base uses $1,184m, already more generous than the FY2025 relationship, and still gives FY2026 free cash flow of $2,926m.
