18. Risks

1. Electrical Americas margin recovery (severe, near-term). Roughly 70% of Electrical Americas revenue is engineered Systems booked into backlog at agreed prices; copper and wage inflation land in cost of sales before pricing resets, and Eaton is ramping two dozen capacity projects that add headcount, depreciation and start-up expense ahead of the volume. Exposure: H1 2026 segment sales grew 18.7% and segment profit 6.3%, an incremental margin of 10.0% against a 26.6% average, with margin down 310 basis points. The full-year guide of 28.8–29.2% needs H2 near 31.2% and a Q4 exit of 32.0–32.5%, which equals the 2030 target four years early from 25.6% three quarters earlier. Leading indicators: the Q3 2026 Electrical Americas margin against the CFO's own 30.0%, the price/cost split given each quarter, COMEX copper, and revenue per day. Evidence the risk is smaller: the realised 190 basis point sequential improvement from Q1 to Q2 2026. Evidence it is larger: Vertiv in 2022 grew revenue 13.9% while operating profit declined 14% on a long-dated backlog priced before the cost inflation, and took six quarters to repair it.

2. Data-centre concentration and the pipeline-to-revenue conversion (severe). Data centres and distributed IT are 21% of company revenue and roughly 29% of Electrical, and the metrics that drive the debate appear only in calls and decks. Conversion timing is management's own: roughly 20% of the 307 GW converts near term with the majority in 2028 and beyond. The unit that converts pipeline to revenue was re-based from a bounded range with an architecture caveat to a single point, a 2.3–2.8x move on the low end. Leading indicators: negotiation-pipeline growth, already decelerated from +81% to +60% on a changed basis; sequential backlog additions, down 41% in Q2 2026; and hyperscaler capital-expenditure guidance.

3. The cancellation disclosure moved to an annual cadence (high). Through Q4 2024 every earnings call included a megaproject tracker with a cancellation rate — "cancellations have been modest, around 10% and well below historical levels" (Q3 2024) — and the word has not been spoken on a call since Q1 2025. Disclosed backlog counts firm orders only and Eaton states plainly that a significant portion of open orders are not firm. Total backlog was $24.1bn at 30 June 2026, about 0.80x trailing revenue, with 71% inside twelve months, about eight and a half months of revenue at the Q2 run-rate. Book-to-bill is a four-quarter average and order growth is trailing twelve months, so both lag a turn by two to three quarters, and the one point-in-time indicator is now annual.

4. Leverage and the acquisition programme (high). Total debt more than doubled in six months to $20,611m, goodwill and other intangibles reached $32,840m against $20,299m of equity, and net leverage moved to 2.9–3.1x from 1.47x. Boyd's allocation is $3,733m of goodwill plus $7,190m of intangibles, is preliminary, and the 10-Q says revisions "could have a material impact." At the raised $1.8bn revenue and the realised 23.1% margin the price is about 23x segment operating profit, before the amortisation of the intangibles it created. The buyback was stopped to fund it. Leading indicators: Boyd revenue against the $1.8bn commitment; Electrical Global goodwill, which nearly doubled to $7,832m, at the annual impairment test; whether the buyback resumes; and the finalisation of the two purchase-price allocations.

5. GAAP earnings decline while revenue accelerates (high). Q2 2026 revenue grew 21% and net income declined 16%; H1 revenue grew 19% and net income declined 13%. The H1 bridge is segment profit +$460m against $160m more amortisation, $204m more net interest and roughly $164m more tax [estimate: H1 2026 pre-tax income taxed at the H1 2025 rate instead of the H1 2026 rate]. Net interest annualises above $800m and amortisation above $1.0bn against FY2025's $486m, and neither flexes with volume. FY2026 guidance is GAAP $10.36–$10.56 against adjusted $13.40–$13.60.

6. The effective tax rate (medium-high). From 17.2% to 28.1% in Q2 and 17.6% to 24.9% in H1, on more income in higher-tax jurisdictions plus $52m of withholding tax on funding Boyd. The FY2025 10-K escalated the stated consequence of an adverse audit outcome from "material unfavorable adjustments to our tax liabilities" to "a material adverse impact on the Company's consolidated financial statements." Because the rate is mix-driven and the mix keeps shifting toward US data-centre revenue, the elevated rate is unlikely to be a one-period item.

7. Dana Reverse Morris Trust execution (medium-high). Eaton distributes Mobility through an exchange offer for SpinCo shares, a SpinCo subsidiary merges into Dana, Eaton shareholders take at least 50.1% of the combined company and Eaton receives roughly $1.1bn of cash. Close is expected Q1 2027 subject to Dana stockholder approval, regulatory approvals and customary conditions, with a plain spin-off as the fallback. The $250m of synergies is roughly 40% of Mobility's own EBITDA on an $11bn combined revenue base, is underwritten by Dana and is scheduled twenty-four months after closing; Eaton shareholders hold the majority of that outcome. Until close, $3,109m of FY2025 revenue and $405m of segment profit stay in continuing operations.

8. Customer concentration, understated by the headline (medium). Six large electrical customers took 22% of FY2025 Electrical sales against eight taking 26% in FY2024, so average exposure per named account rose to its highest in six years even as the headline declined. The descriptor changed from "distributors" to "customers" in the FY2021 10-K, consistent with the shift to direct accounts. Aerospace: 20% to three aircraft OEMs. eMobility: 18% to one OEM, from 27% to three a year earlier. No single customer exceeded 10% of consolidated sales in 2023, 2024 or 2025.

9. Supplier single-sourcing and skilled labour (medium). Both were added in FY2025. Verbatim: "We also maintain single-source supplier relationships because either alternative sources are not available, or the relationship is advantageous... The effect of unavailability or delivery delays would be more severe if associated with our higher volume and more profitable products." And: "We have in the past experienced, and could in the future experience, shortages for skilled or unskilled labor, which has in the past and could in the future negatively impact our growth and results of operations." Neither is quantified, and the Item 1 raw-materials paragraph still states Eaton has no difficulty obtaining raw materials under normal circumstances.

10. Competitive entry (medium). Added in the FY2025 risk factors, where the end-market volatility factor gained the words "newly competitive market players", the first time in ten years of filings that competitive entry is named as a profitability risk. Vertiv grew from $4,998m of revenue in FY2021 to $10,230m in FY2025 and guides FY2026 to roughly $14.0bn; GE Vernova, nVent, Hubbell, Schneider and Legrand are all adding electrical capacity into the same demand.

11. The 800-volt DC transition (medium). If the architecture shifts and content per megawatt does not hold, the unit that converts gigawatts to revenue falls with it. NVIDIA's own claims for the architecture — 157% more power on the same wire gauge, eliminated conversion stages, a 26% smaller rack converter — each reduce physical content in the layer Eaton sells. FY2024 added the technology-disruption risk factor, the only mention of "data center" anywhere in Eaton's risk factors, and FY2025 retained it while softening "cutting edge technology" to "innovative technology."

12. Free cash flow conversion against the 2030 commitment (medium). FY2025 was about 75% and the FY2026 guide implies about 78% against a 95–100% commitment, while capex stays elevated and working capital builds — inventory $4,721m to $5,417m and receivables $5,387m to $6,673m in six months. H1 2026 free cash flow was $1,188m, so 69–72% of the full-year guide must land in H2.

13. Supply-chain finance inside payables (low-medium). Obligations rose 68% in eighteen months to $669m inside payables of $5,421m, so payables and working-capital ratios are not comparable to peers without adjustment.

14. Environmental and legal (low). 103 sites worldwide including Superfund sites at end-2025, none individually significant, with a $69m undiscounted accrual. Legal contingencies include claims from historic products that may have contained asbestos, with no separate accrual disclosed. At the disclosed levels this is immaterial against $27,448m of revenue.

How these combine. A bad quarter would run them together. Copper stays elevated into Q4, so the 300 basis points of price/cost in the H2 bridge lands partially and the 28.8–29.2% guide is missed for the second cut in three quarters. A hyperscaler pushes a project, so the near-term 20% of the pipeline converts more slowly, and because book-to-bill is a four-quarter average the reported signal arrives two to three quarters after the fact with the cancellation rate now annual. The twelve ramped plants hold fixed cost against lower volume and incremental margin, already 10.0% in H1 2026, compresses further. Net interest above $800m and amortisation above $1.0bn are fixed, so GAAP earnings decline faster with the buyback suspended. And Boyd's $10,923m of goodwill and intangibles, both preliminary, face impairment testing against a decelerated data-centre forecast in a segment whose goodwill nearly doubled in one quarter. A second correlation runs across years: in Q1 2025 tariffs cost 80 basis points of Electrical Americas margin guidance and 40 of company guidance, recovered "on a dollar-for-dollar basis", which restores dollars and dilutes percentage margin; in Q1 2026 commodities cost 100 and 50 basis points, framed the same way.

Ten years of risk-factor drift. Item 1A ran 1,433 words in FY2016, 2,065 in FY2024 and 3,900 in FY2025, the largest rewrite of the ten years. FY2025 added seven factors: acquisitions and integration, placed first under operational risks; reliance on suppliers including single-source relationships; artificial intelligence; employee attraction and retention, absent for six years; spin-off completion; geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty; and US government contracting. It escalated the tax factor's stated consequence, merged the two inflation factors and broadened them, and retreated on climate — the factor was retitled "Weather disruptions and regulatory, market and social reactions to them", and the 2030 carbon-neutral commitment, the metals-scarcity point and the sentence "we believe Eaton is well positioned to capitalize on secular trends and market opportunities arising from these risks" are all gone. Earlier: FY2017 deleted the Irish-domicile factor, the only year "Ireland" or "Irish" appears in Item 1A; FY2024 added the technology-disruption and trade-policy factors and deleted COVID-19. Neither backlog nor customer concentration has appeared in Item 1A in any of the ten filings.

19. Source disclosure

Primary sources. Ten Eaton annual reports on Form 10-K, FY2016 through FY2025, filed 22 February 2017 to 26 February 2026, and six quarterly reports on Form 10-Q covering 2024-Q3 through 2026-Q2, filed 31 July 2026 for the latest. Forty-three earnings-call transcripts, contiguous from Q4 2015 to Q2 2026. Thirty-eight presentation and conference transcripts from 26 February 2016 to 11 June 2026, including the analyst and investor days of 2016, 2017, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2025, the UBS Global Industrials conference of 2 December 2025, the Barclays Industrial Select conference of 17 February 2026, and the Dana and Eaton merger call of 11 June 2026. Eleven investor decks with rendered slides, 2 March 2020 through 31 July 2026. Twenty-four SEC earnings releases (8-K Exhibit 99), Q3 2020 through Q2 2026, which are the source for every quarterly figure. Nine DEF 14A proxy statements, 2018 through 2026, covering FY2017 through FY2025 compensation. Ninety-two Form 4 filings covering February 2025 to August 2026.

Peer and value-chain filings. Thirty-three companies' 10-K and 10-Q filings were used for the comparisons in §3, §4, §5 and §12: Vertiv, Hubbell, nVent, GE Vernova, Generac, Powell, Rockwell, Emerson, Parker-Hannifin, Honeywell and Honeywell Aerospace, Illinois Tool Works, Dover, RTX, TransDigm, HEICO, Moog, Woodward, Curtiss-Wright, Dana, BorgWarner, Allison, American Axle, Cummins, PACCAR, WESCO, Freeport-McMoRan, Cleveland-Cliffs, Amphenol, Quanta, Equinix, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta. Peer income-statement, balance-sheet and cash-flow series were computed from SEC XBRL company facts, accessed 17 August 2026. Fiscal years differ: Emerson, Rockwell, TransDigm, Woodward, Moog and Powell end in September, HEICO in October and Parker in June, so their "latest quarter" is the three months to 31 March 2026 and their FY2025 covers a different twelve months from Eaton's.

Market and consensus data. Bloomberg BEst consensus for adjusted EPS, revenue and operating profit, snapshot as of 14 August 2026; every Eaton consensus series shares that one as-of date, and it postdates Eaton's 31 July 2026 print. Twenty-two weekly Bloomberg snapshots reconstruct a dated consensus path back to 18 April 2025. Daily price, dividend and total-return series from Yahoo Finance, 13,665 sessions, pulled 17 August 2026; that series reproduces Bloomberg's own year-to-date and twelve-month return fields and its price for Eaton exactly at 14 August 2026. Quarterly EPS and revenue consensus, estimate dispersion and price targets from the Nasdaq earnings-surprise service, Yahoo's analyst panel and stockanalysis.com. Twelve Third Bridge expert interviews, dated 2022 to July 2026, on the Mobility segment.

Series assembled from those sources. A ten-year annual financial series and a twelve-quarter series reconciled to the filings; a peer financial panel; a daily forward-price-to-earnings and price-to-book series; a dated consensus-revision path; a drawdown and earnings-reaction series; an annual multiples table; a public comparable-company table; and a seven-year driver-based operating model with three scenarios.

Gaps and failures. The Bloomberg terminal was running but not serving data on the pull date, so no fresh snapshot could be taken and no BEst EBITDA, GAAP EPS or capex series was obtainable. That leaves eleven of the thirty-three public-comparable columns absent (§16), the forward EBITDA, capex and cash-flow cells of §13.1 blank, and no forward EV/EBITDA anywhere. Contemporaneous consensus before April 2025 is not recoverable, so every forward multiple quoted for an earlier date uses realised next-twelve-month adjusted EPS and is labelled perfect-foresight. Quarterly consensus for Q3 2023, Q1 2024 and Q2 2024, and quarterly revenue consensus before Q3 2024, are shown blank. No sell-side research covers Eaton in the local digest, so the only analyst ratings and targets here are the aggregator figures cited in §14 and §15. The risk-factor comparison covers Item 1A across FY2016–FY2025; Item 1 and the MD&A were not compared. Third Bridge expert interviews cover Mobility only. No coded external dataset covers the electrical franchise (Appendix C). Three primary documents could not be retrieved: the Dana 8-K exhibit and merger agreement, which returned an HTTP 403; the Cummins joint-venture note; and Graybar Electric's 10-K, which files with the SEC but has no exchange ticker. The earliest filing on hand is the FY2016 10-K and the earliest transcript Q4 2015, so Cooper Industries in 2012 is sourced from public reporting and the 2008–09 downturn is outside every series used here. Coverage of Eaton's own filings stops at the 31 July 2026 print.

Data-quality corrections. The SEC XBRL extract for Eaton reports annual revenue as zero for FY2010–FY2016 and basic and diluted EPS as zero for every year FY2010–FY2025; leaves operating income blank from FY2020; reports stock-based compensation of $5–14m against $126m actual in FY2025; and mixes six-month and quarterly bases in its 2026 cash-flow columns. Every figure above comes from the filings. The XBRL row labelled "Long-Term Debt" includes the current portion, so FY2025 net debt is $9,092m and not $10,228m, and FY2025 leverage is 1.47x and not 1.7x. The XBRL equity-statement repurchase tag reports $286m for FY2023, repeating FY2022, in a year Eaton repurchased nothing. Boyd Thermal closed on 12 March 2026, inside Q1, not in Q2; a figure computed on a Q2 close understates Boyd's contribution by about six weeks. Adjusted EPS for FY2016–FY2018 ($4.22, $4.65, $5.39) is recoverable from Eaton's own Q4 8-K exhibits and is on the pre-2021 definition. FY2019 adjusted EPS has two published values, $5.76 as first reported and $5.67 in the FY2020 comparative column, and the table in §13.1 uses the figure published for the year.

Discrepancies left unresolved. The two Boyd headcount figures — "more than 5,000" in the FY2025 10-K and the Q2 2026 10-Q against "more than 6,000" in the Q1 2026 10-Q. The Boyd 2026 revenue figure, "meet or exceed the 2026 revenues of $1.7 billion" on the Q4 2025 call against $1.8bn from Q2 2026. The two Mobility EBITDA bases, Eaton's reported FY2025 $528m against Dana's 2026 estimate of $614m, a gap of $86–106m that neither party bridged. Dana's own two revenue-mix cuts inside one presentation, 65/35 with a 25% aftermarket on page 6 against 42/34/24 on page 9. Two price-target lows published the same week, $333 and $321. Bloomberg's CY2027 consensus EPS of $15.82 against Yahoo's panel at $16.02 on 22 estimates. And the as-reported EBITDA in each year's earnings release differs from the restated series used in §13 and §15 by up to 1%. Seven further conflicts sit inside this document and no source here settles them. The return-on-capital-employed column in §3.1 does not recompute from the NOPAT and capital-employed columns printed beside it in five of its eight rows — FY2018 gives 10.1% against the 9.8% shown and FY2025 gives 13.6% against 13.8%, and the 13.8% FY2025 figure is the one used throughout. Revenue per shipping day rose 25% from the start of 2025 on management's own figure and 29% on the per-day figures derived in §1.4 ($48.6m to $62.7m); the 25% figure is used in the text. FY2025 data-centre revenue appears as $5,764m where the disclosed 21% end-market share is applied to sales and as $4.6–4.9bn inside the per-megawatt estimates, the second excluding distributed IT; the two are not reconciled anywhere. The ten-year cash-paid-for-acquisitions row in §10.4 sums to $8,031m against the $8,029m total used in §7, §10.4 and §11, so one annual cell is $2m out. Dana's FY2025 EBITDA margin appears at 6.5% in §3.3 and §8, at 8.9% segment EBITDA in §4.3 and at 8.1% adjusted in Appendix B, on three different bases. Total company backlog at 31 December 2025 is $19.8bn in §5, §13.4 and §13.5 against $19.6bn on Eaton's own Q4 2025 slide and $19,596m as the sum of the three disclosed segment figures. And FY2026 consensus adjusted EPS is $13.49 on the Bloomberg snapshot against a $13.51 mean across 23 analysts on the aggregator panel, the same split as the CY2027 $15.82 against $16.02 above; the Bloomberg series is used in every table.

Web sources. Roughly forty-five pages across about thirty domains support the [web]-tagged claims, and every one appears in Appendix B with its link and access date. The largest groups are competitor results releases and presentations (abb.com, se.com, vertiv.com, legrand.com, siemens.com), trade and technical press (semianalysis.com, spectrum.ieee.org, trendforce.com, datacenterfrontier.com, getuniqcli.com, fleetowner.com, fleetequipmentmag.com), primary technical publishers (developer.nvidia.com, eaton.com product literature, abb.com product literature, ls-electric.com), research houses reported second-hand (delloro.com, woodmac.com, emp.lbl.gov, constructconnect via trade press), aggregators used only for price and estimate context (stockanalysis.com, investing.com, macrotrends-class services), and one paywalled independent analysis (electroneconomics.substack.com) whose title and framing are cited and whose body is behind the paywall. Market-research aggregators are used only for order-of-magnitude context and are named as such where they appear. No claim depends on web material that could not be verified.

Estimates. Roughly forty figures are tagged [estimate:] and each states its method and its bounds where it appears. By method: nine apply Eaton's disclosed whole-percentage end-market or channel mix to reported sales; eight derive a per-unit economic figure by dividing disclosed segment revenue by an external volume series; seven reconstruct capital-structure, leverage or share-count figures from the balance sheet and disclosed deal terms; six convert a disclosed capacity or pipeline figure into revenue at a stated capture range; four straight-line disclosed purchase-price intangibles to reconstruct segment amortisation and returns; three invert a disclosed margin bridge against published input prices; and three adjust published consensus for the pending Mobility separation. Every one is medium confidence at best, and each is quoted with its bounds.

20. What we still don't know, and what would resolve it

Ten open items, most material first, each with the metric that would settle it.

  1. What Eaton looks like in an actual downturn. How far revenue and margin would decline in a downcycle is not established. Eaton's own record includes a 12.4% revenue decline from $22,552m in FY2014 to $19,747m in FY2016 and a second decline in 2020, Electrical Americas backlog is 1.05x annual segment revenue, the 10-K states a significant portion of open orders are not firm, and the cancellation rate moved to an annual cadence after Q1 2025. Resolved by: a quarter of negative sequential backlog additions, or a restated cancellation rate.

  2. What sets Electrical Global's margin. At $6,815m of FY2025 sales, 25% of company revenue and larger than Aerospace, its 19.4% margin has not moved in five years, and whether the gap to Electrical Americas is mix, channel or a structural ceiling is unknown. Boyd, the fastest-growing acquisition, reports through it. Resolved by: regional revenue and margin for Europe, Asia Pacific and Global Energy Infrastructure, and a Boyd-versus-legacy margin split.

  3. Whether the orders measure end demand or channel position. Six unnamed customers took 22% of FY2025 Electrical sales through a primarily two-step channel, and Eaton reports 41% trailing organic order growth. Whether those six are distributors or end users decides which one the order book measures. Resolved by: distributor sell-through at WESCO, Rexel and Sonepar against Eaton's shipments into the channel.

  4. Eaton's realised revenue per megawatt of data-centre capacity. The disclosed unit is an accessible-content figure; §1.4 bounds the realised figure at $0.21–0.32m/MW by inference and §6.3 bounds the capture rate at 8–17%. Resolved by: a disclosed data-centre revenue figure divided by a disclosed megawatt figure, neither of which Eaton publishes.

  5. Whether the tax-rate step is permanent. The effective rate moved from 17.6% to 24.9% across one half and 28.1% in Q2 2026 alone. Roughly seven points of effective rate on FY2026 pre-tax income is about $1.30 of adjusted EPS, which decides whether the 2030 earnings plan is arithmetically available. The one-off withholding tax on funding Boyd, jurisdictional earnings mix and the Irish and EU 15% minimum-tax regime are not separated anywhere. Resolved by: the FY2026 tax footnote's jurisdictional reconciliation.

  6. What share of Electrical revenue is service, retrofit and aftermarket, and what its renewal rate is. Management names the service network as one of five requirements to win 800-volt DC work; Eaton discloses no service revenue line, attach rate or retention figure, and the Products/Systems split is a manufacturing classification. Both the durability assessment in §3.1 and the cyclical amplitude applied to 73% of revenue in §17 turn on it.

  7. The separate margins of Products and Systems. Systems is 76% of Electrical Americas revenue and all of its growth; the two-equation solve fails because the Americas-versus-Global gap dominates it. If Systems is the lower-margin half, the margin path in §17 inverts as backlog converts. The same split is doing duty as the labelled proxy for the undisclosed negotiated-versus-rollup mix.

  8. Where Eaton manufactures, and how much of the bill of materials crosses a tariffed border. Item 2 states only that Eaton operates approximately 201 locations in 36 countries, so the "2M+ additional square footage" capacity programme cannot be sized against the existing base and the Section 232 copper exposure cannot be measured.

  9. What Eaton receives for Mobility and what it leaves behind. The at-least-50.1% Dana stake is not sized against Mobility's contribution; whether the tax-matters agreement restricts Eaton's own repurchases after close is not addressed in any Eaton filing, while §17 assumes buybacks resume in 2027; and the stranded corporate cost left when 10% of revenue exits is not estimated. Mobility's standalone cost of sales, working capital and operating cash flow are unknown from any source. Resolved by: SpinCo's Form 10 and Dana's S-4 carve-out financials.

  10. Where the industry's capacity additions land, and when the price/cost gap stops being temporary. The announced capacity additions of Schneider, ABB, Siemens, Vertiv and GE Vernova are not assembled into the same demand pool, and supply catching demand is the condition under which Electrical pricing reverses inside the forecast window. Resolved by: the Q3 2026 Electrical Americas margin against the CFO's own 30.0%, and each rival's capex disclosure.

Four further items are unresolved and smaller. No post-Boyd rating action is disclosed anywhere, so the cost-of-debt and refinancing work in §12 depends on agency positions taken before a $9.5bn cash deal closed. The useful lives assigned to Boyd's $7,190m of intangibles are not published, unlike every prior deal of scale, so the annual amortisation cannot be checked against Boyd's segment profit. The megaproject win rate of about 40% is the parameter that converts a $3.0trn announced backlog into Eaton revenue and the deck does not define whether it means bids won, project value captured or electrical content share. And whether Eaton's 50% interest in Eaton Cummins Automated Transmission Technologies transfers to SpinCo is not stated in any filing or on the merger call, which decides whether the acquirer receives the North American automated-transmission franchise or the components around it.

Metrics to monitor. Electrical Americas segment margin against 30.0% in Q3 2026 and 32.0–32.5% in Q4. Sequential backlog additions, which declined 41% in Q2 2026. Negotiation-pipeline growth and the basis it is quoted on. Quarterly customer orders as given on the call, distinct from the trailing figure in the 10-Q. Data-centre revenue growth against the 17% rate inside the 2030 plan. The first 800-volt DC order, guided to H2 2026. Boyd revenue against the $1.8bn commitment and Electrical Global goodwill of $7,832m at the annual impairment test. Free cash flow against the $3.9–4.3bn guide, of which 69–72% must land in H2 2026. The GAAP effective tax rate. And whether the buyback resumes in 2027.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

Disclosures that appear only in the decks.

  • Content per megawatt has a published definition, and it is a range anchored to a share of site capex. The March 2025 investor day gives Eaton potential sales per megawatt of $1.2–1.5m for a traditional data centre at 6–10% of total compute and infrastructure capex, and $1.2–2.9m for an AI data centre at 6–14% [deck: Investor Conference 2025, 2025-03-11, slide 67]. The calls give no definition. At 6–14% of capex, the $3.4m figure implies $24–57m of total build capex per megawatt against the $20–29m the deck's own range implies. Informs §1, §6 and §8.
  • The grey-space and white-space split is assigned product by product, and only in the deck [slide 66]: grey space is medium- and low-voltage switchgear, transformers, medium-voltage busway, pad-mount switchgear, the modular power centre and fire signalling; white space is UPS, power distribution units, racks and rack-mounted distribution and connectivity, cabinets, low-voltage busway, the stand-alone power unit, Brightlayer and engineering services. Informs §1 and §4.
  • The order book in dollars. Total backlog went $4.2bn (2019) to $19.6bn (2025) with the Electrical and Aerospace split by year, and the Electrical Americas negotiations pipeline went $2.4bn (2019) to $9.8bn (2025), a 26% compound rate [deck: Q4 2025 earnings, 2026-02-03, slide 9]. Every call reference to the pipeline is a growth rate; this is the only disclosure of the dollar amount, which at 0.74x a year of segment sales stands alongside the $15.2bn backlog and may overlap it. Informs §1 and §13.5.
  • The megaproject conversion parameters. As of Q4 2025: a $3.0trn North America backlog across 866 announced projects, $937bn announced in the year, 30% year-over-year backlog growth, only about 16% of projects started, a cancellation rate of about 13%, and an Eaton win rate of about 40% [deck: Q4 2025 earnings, slide 8]. The deck does not define the win rate. Informs §4 and §20.
  • Product-level growth outlooks. About 50% a year for the 9395XR three-phase UPS, about 17% for the vacuum fault interrupter transformer and about 12% for utility underground switchgear [deck: Investor Conference 2025, slides 68 and 77]. Informs §2.
  • Named partnerships that address the interconnection constraint. Siemens Energy for integrated on-site generation with "no external power dependency, shorter project timeline and operational flexibility"; NVIDIA for high-voltage DC supporting 1 MW racks; ChargePoint for EV charging [deck: Q2 2025 earnings, 2025-08-05, slide 7]. The NVIDIA relationship then produced the Eaton Beam Rubin DSX platform, a pre-engineered grid-to-chip power and cooling blueprint scalable from megawatts to 100-plus megawatts [deck: Q1 2026 earnings, 2026-05-05, slide 7]. Informs §2 and §5.
  • Rank claims appear for the first time in February 2026: number one in US power conversion equipment, number one or two in low- and medium-voltage electrical equipment, number one or two in aerospace hydraulic and fuel pumps, number one in Americas commercial truck transmission and clutches [deck: Q4 2025 earnings, slide 5]. The 10-K describes the basis of competition and lists no rank, and the slide cites no source. Informs §3 and §4.
  • The acquisition hurdle was lowered in the decks themselves. The 2020 deck sets "target minimum returns of 300 bps above cost of capital" and accretion after two years [slide 134]; the 2025 deck sets "target return of 200-300 bps above cost of capital" [slide 30]. Informs §10 and §11.
  • The 2030 revenue bridge already assumed Mobility would shrink or leave. Electrical at $31bn-plus and Aerospace at about $6bn sum to roughly $37bn against the about-$38bn company target, leaving roughly $1bn for Vehicle and eMobility, which were $3.5bn in 2024 [deck: Investor Conference 2025, slides 15, 80, 105, 113]. The separation was announced ten months later. The deck also shows about $21bn of acquisition capacity on top of the organic figure, so its own arithmetic makes acquisitions the larger swing factor in the 2030 outcome. Informs §14 and §17.
  • The eMobility forward disclosure ran to its horizon and can be scored. The March 2022 deck showed eMobility reaching $1.2bn by 2025 at about 11% operating margin with the 2025 bar labelled "Booked ~87%" [deck: Investor Conference 2022, 2022-03-01, slide 20]. FY2025 delivered $604m with a $14m operating loss. That is the same kind of management-defined, unaudited forward figure as the backlog and negotiations pipeline, and it delivered roughly half. Informs §2 and §8.
  • Management's own valuation slide, published once. The 2020 deck closes the CFO section with an EV/EBITDA bar chart placing Eaton third from the bottom of thirteen peers, as of 26 February 2020 [slide 138]. It has no successor in the 2021, 2022 or 2025 decks.

Appendix C — External data sources

Two external datasets are available for a company of Eaton's type. Neither is pulled here.

Installed fleet (mosaic). A picture of the commercial and military aircraft fleet assembled from several public and paid sources: units in service by type and operator, fleet age distribution, and orders and backlog at the airframers. Cirium is the paid backbone and the FAA registry is a free partial substitute. It measures the denominator behind Eaton's Aerospace aftermarket — the population of aircraft fitted with Eaton content that generate shop visits — and the forward OEM ship-set volume behind the commercial and military original-equipment channels. It would strengthen §1's Aerospace driver tree, where commercial aftermarket revenue per active aircraft-year is currently estimated at $19–24k against an all-aircraft denominator, and §4.2, where Eaton's 4.6% share of the listed systems set is measured on revenue and not on installed content. The mosaic is partial. Not pulled.

EIA Open Data. The US Energy Information Administration's public API for energy prices, production, consumption and electric-power series, updated on the schedule of each underlying release. Its relevance to Eaton is the grid and utility demand backdrop: electricity generation, capacity additions and retail power prices. It would strengthen §6, where the utility driver's stated ultimate exposure is approved distribution rate base and grid-hardening spend and is currently measured against no independent series, and §1.3's Driver 3. Free, and it needs an API key. Not pulled.

Neither dataset measures the electrical franchise that accounts for 73% of revenue and 79% of segment profit. The series that would — US Census value of construction put in place for the data-centre and non-residential categories, producer price indices for switchgear and for power distribution and specialty transformers, exchange copper prices, and utility distribution capital expenditure — are named in §20 as what would resolve the open items on Drivers 2 and 3.
